Vibe Sparking

OpenClaw Security Lesson 1: Changing Default Port — From Public Target to Stealth Deployment

Section titled “OpenClaw Security Lesson 1: Changing Default Port — From Public Target to Stealth Deployment”

Introduction: Why Default Ports Are Security Risks?

Section titled “Introduction: Why Default Ports Are Security Risks?”

In cybersecurity, default configurations are often the biggest security vulnerabilities. OpenClaw’s default port 18789 is a classic example. This port number is documented in official documentation, tutorials, and README files, making it a public target for automated scanners.

📊 Real Threat Data

Section titled “📊 Real Threat Data”
  • 330,000+ OpenClaw instances exposed to public internet - According to real-time monitoring site openclaw.allegro.earth
  • Shodan search results: product:"OpenClaw" port:18789 returns thousands of exposed instances
  • Masscan scanning cost: masscan 0.0.0.0/0 -p18789 --rate=10000 can scan the entire internet in hours
  • Public exploit tools: Tools like OpenClaw-PwnKit can directly obtain reverse shells

Step 1: Understanding Risk Principles

Section titled “Step 1: Understanding Risk Principles”

1.1 How Automated Scanning Works

Section titled “1.1 How Automated Scanning Works”

Attackers use automated tools to scan specific ports at extremely low cost:

1.2 Why is Port 18789 So Dangerous?

Section titled “1.2 Why is Port 18789 So Dangerous?”
  1. Public information: Port number explicitly marked in official documentation
  2. Concentrated target: All OpenClaw users share the same port
  3. Low scanning cost: Scanning single port vs full port range
  4. High success rate: Almost everything found is an OpenClaw instance

Step 2: Solution — Changing Default Port

Section titled “Step 2: Solution — Changing Default Port”

2.1 Principles for Choosing New Port

Section titled “2.1 Principles for Choosing New Port”
  1. Range: 20000-65535 (avoid common service ports)
  2. Avoid conflicts: Don’t use 22(SSH), 80(HTTP), 443(HTTPS), 3306(MySQL), etc.
  3. Recommended port: 28800 (easy to remember, low conflict probability)
  4. Randomness: Consider random ports for increased stealth

2.2 Modifying Configuration File

Section titled “2.2 Modifying Configuration File”

Edit OpenClaw configuration file ~/.openclaw/openclaw.json:

Key configuration notes:

  • port: New port number
  • bind: “loopback” restricts listening to local loopback address, avoiding public exposure

Bare metal deployment:

Section titled “2.4 Updating Client Configurations”

Step 3: Verifying Modification Effectiveness

Section titled “Step 3: Verifying Modification Effectiveness”

3.1 Local Verification

Section titled “3.1 Local Verification”

3.2 External Scan Verification

Section titled “3.2 External Scan Verification”

3.3 Shodan Monitoring Verification

Section titled “3.3 Shodan Monitoring Verification”
  1. Immediate check: ip:YOUR_PUBLIC_IP port:18789
  2. After 24-48 hours: Check again to confirm disappearance from Shodan index
  3. New port check: ip:YOUR_PUBLIC_IP port:28800 (should not be indexed)

Step 4: Cost-Benefit Analysis

Section titled “Step 4: Cost-Benefit Analysis”
MetricAssessment
Time required5-10 minutes
Technical difficultyBeginner (configuration file modification)
Risk levelZero risk (can revert anytime)
Security effectivenessBlocks 90%+ automated scanning
Stealth effectivenessDisappears from public scanning radars like Shodan
LimitationsDoesn’t protect against targeted attacks, internal attacks, application-layer vulnerabilities

4.1 Why This is Effective?

Section titled “4.1 Why This is Effective?”
  1. Economic principle: Attacker scanning cost vs benefit ratio
  2. Statistical principle: Very low probability of non-standard ports being scanned
  3. Psychological principle: Attackers tend to look for low-hanging fruit

4.2 Real Case Comparison

Section titled “4.2 Real Case Comparison”

Before modification:

  • Exposed in pool of 330,000+ instances
  • Faces hundreds of automated scans daily
  • Potential target for vulnerability exploitation tools

After modification:

  • Disappears from public scanning radars
  • Scanning cost increases 65,535x (full port scan vs single port scan)
  • Attackers need targeted probing

Step 5: Advanced Security Recommendations

Section titled “Step 5: Advanced Security Recommendations”

5.1 Combining with Other Security Measures

Section titled “5.1 Combining with Other Security Measures”
  1. Firewall rules: Restrict source IP access
  2. Reverse proxy: Hide real port behind Nginx/Apache proxy
  3. VPN/Tailscale: Access only within internal network or encrypted channels
  4. Authentication strengthening: Enable token authentication, IP whitelisting

5.2 Monitoring and Alerting

Section titled “5.2 Monitoring and Alerting”

5.3 Regular Security Audits

Section titled “5.3 Regular Security Audits”
  1. Monthly checks: Shodan, Censys, and other public scanning results
  2. Port scanning: Regularly scan your own public IP
  3. Configuration review: Check if security configurations were accidentally modified

Frequently Asked Questions

Section titled “Frequently Asked Questions”

Q1: Will changing port affect OpenClaw functionality?

Section titled “Q1: Will changing port affect OpenClaw functionality?”

A: No. All OpenClaw functions are based on HTTP API, port is just the access entry point.

Q2: Do all clients need to be modified?

Section titled “Q2: Do all clients need to be modified?”

A: Yes, all clients connecting to OpenClaw via HTTP need port updates.

Q3: Can I use randomly generated ports?

Section titled “Q3: Can I use randomly generated ports?”

A: Yes, but ensure client configurations are synchronized and recorded in a secure location.

Q4: What if connection issues occur after modification?

Section titled “Q4: What if connection issues occur after modification?”

A: Troubleshooting steps:

  1. Confirm Gateway process is running normally
  2. Verify port listening status
  3. Check firewall rules
  4. Revert to original configuration for testing

Q5: Is this the only security measure needed?

Section titled “Q5: Is this the only security measure needed?”

A: No. Changing default port is the first step in basic security hardening, should be combined with other security measures for defense in depth.

Summary

Section titled “Summary”

Changing OpenClaw’s default port is a low-cost, zero-risk, high-return security hardening measure. Through this simple change, you can:

  1. ✅ Immediately reduce 90%+ automated attack risk
  2. ✅ Disappear from public scanning radars
  3. ✅ Increase attacker probing costs
  4. ✅ Lay foundation for subsequent security hardening

Security is not a one-time task, but an ongoing process. Start by changing the default port, then gradually build a complete security protection system.

This is Lesson 1 of the OpenClaw Security Hardening Series. Subsequent lessons will cover advanced topics like SSH security, authentication hardening, network isolation, etc.

Action recommendation: Immediately check your OpenClaw instance. If still using default port 18789, follow this guide to modify it.

Claude Code 2.1.98 Deep Dive: Enterprise Security Overhaul & Native Perforce Support

Apr 10, 2026
Vibe Sparking

Claude Code 2.1.98 In-Depth Analysis

Section titled “Claude Code 2.1.98 In-Depth Analysis”

Release date: April 2026 (extracted from CHANGELOG.md) Previous version: 2.1.97 | Analysis generated: 2026-04-10

Overview

Section titled “Overview”

2.1.98 is a major update containing 8 new features and 40+ fixes and improvements. Core themes:

  1. Enhanced enterprise platform support — Google Vertex AI guided setup, Perforce integration
  2. Security overhaul — Multiple Bash permission bypass vulnerabilities fixed (CVE-level)
  3. Stability polish — Numerous edge case fixes for /resume, MCP, and the permissions system
  4. Developer experience improvements — Monitor tool, Vim mode enhancements, OTEL tracing refinements

I. New Features in Detail

Section titled “I. New Features in Detail”

1.1 Google Vertex AI Interactive Setup Wizard

Section titled “1.1 Google Vertex AI Interactive Setup Wizard”

What changed: After selecting “3rd-party platform” on the login screen, a complete GCP guided flow is now available — authentication, project/region selection, credential verification, and model binding all in one step.

Background: Previously, configuring Vertex AI required manually setting multiple environment variables (ANTHROPIC_VERTEX_PROJECT_ID, CLOUD_ML_REGION, etc.), creating a high barrier for users unfamiliar with GCP and making configuration errors hard to troubleshoot.

Use cases:

  • Enterprise users deploying Claude Code on GCP for the first time
  • New team members onboarding quickly without reading configuration docs
  • Switching between multiple projects/regions directly through the wizard

Notes:

  • Requires gcloud CLI to be installed locally with basic authentication completed
  • Region selection affects latency and model availability (some models are only available in regions like us-east5)
  • Model pinning writes to local configuration; switching requires re-running the wizard

Comparison with similar products:

  • Codex CLI: Relies on OpenAI API key with no platform wizard — configuration is relatively simple
  • Gemini CLI: A native Google product that works after gcloud auth with no extra configuration needed
  • This update narrows the experience gap between Claude Code and Gemini CLI within the GCP ecosystem

Historical context: 2.1.94 added Bedrock Mantle support; 2.1.97 fixed Bedrock SigV4 authentication issues. The Vertex AI wizard continues the cloud platform integration strategy.

1.2 Perforce Mode (CLAUDE_CODE_PERFORCE_MODE)

Section titled “1.2 Perforce Mode (CLAUDE_CODE_PERFORCE_MODE)”

What changed: When this environment variable is set, Edit/Write/NotebookEdit will throw an error and prompt p4 edit when encountering read-only files, instead of silently overwriting them.

Background: Large-scale game development, chip design, and other industries widely use Perforce (P4) for version control. P4’s workflow is fundamentally different from Git — files are read-only by default and must be checked out (p4 edit) before modification. AI coding tools that directly overwrite read-only files can cause lost changes and corrupted workspace states.

Use cases:

  • Game studios working on large projects with Unreal Engine + P4
  • Chip RTL code repositories (typically 100GB+ P4 depots)
  • Any hybrid Git + P4 workflow

Notes:

  • Requires setting CLAUDE_CODE_PERFORCE_MODE=1 in your shell profile or project .env
  • Currently only blocks writes and prompts the user — does not automatically run p4 edit (likely a security consideration)
  • Works best with P4’s .p4config files

Comparison with similar products:

  • Codex CLI / Gemini CLI: Neither supports Perforce; P4 users must handle this themselves
  • Claude Code is the first AI coding tool with native Perforce workflow support — a differentiating advantage in the enterprise market

Future evolution: Subsequent versions may add automatic p4 edit capability (with permission confirmation) and P4 changelist integration.

1.3 Monitor Tool — Background Script Event Stream

Section titled “1.3 Monitor Tool — Background Script Event Stream”

What changed: A new Monitor tool that can stream events from background scripts in real time.

Background: Claude Code already supported running scripts in the background (subagents, long-running builds, etc.), but previously lacked real-time monitoring — you could only wait for completion or poll logs.

Use cases:

  • Monitoring progress of long-running test suites
  • Watching real-time output from background build/deploy scripts
  • Debugging anomalies during subagent execution

Notes:

  • Works even better alongside the 2.1.98 fix for “background subagent failures not reporting partial progress”
  • Event stream format may change between versions

Comparison with similar products:

  • Codex CLI: Supports --stream output but has no standalone monitoring tool
  • Gemini CLI: No background task monitoring capability yet

1.4 Subprocess Sandbox Hardening (PID Namespace Isolation)

Section titled “1.4 Subprocess Sandbox Hardening (PID Namespace Isolation)”

What changed:

  • On Linux, setting CLAUDE_CODE_SUBPROCESS_ENV_SCRUB enables PID namespace isolation
  • New CLAUDE_CODE_SCRIPT_CAPS limits the number of script invocations per session

Background: As Claude Code is used in increasingly sensitive environments (production servers, CI/CD), subprocess isolation requirements grow stronger. PID namespaces prevent subprocesses from seeing or manipulating other processes on the host.

Use cases:

  • Restricting Claude Code subprocess permissions in CI/CD pipelines
  • Security isolation in multi-tenant environments
  • Limiting script executions per session to prevent runaway loops

Notes:

  • PID namespaces are Linux-only (macOS doesn’t support this kernel feature)
  • Requires root or CAP_SYS_ADMIN privileges to create namespaces
  • The CLAUDE_CODE_SCRIPT_CAPS limit needs tuning based on your workload

Comparison with similar products:

  • Codex CLI: Uses Docker containers for isolation — coarser-grained but more mature
  • Gemini CLI: No explicit sandbox mechanism yet
  • Claude Code’s approach is more lightweight, suitable for environments where Docker isn’t available

1.5 Print Mode Cross-User Cache Optimization

Section titled “1.5 Print Mode Cross-User Cache Optimization”

What changed: New --exclude-dynamic-system-prompt-sections flag that excludes dynamic system prompt sections in print mode.

Background: Claude Code’s print mode is used for batch/automation scenarios. Dynamic portions of system prompts (usernames, timestamps, etc.) prevent prompt cache sharing across different users, wasting tokens.

Use cases:

  • Enterprise batch code review pipelines
  • Reducing API costs in multi-user shared CI services
  • Prompt cache hit rate optimization

Notes:

  • Excluded sections may contain useful context — weigh the trade-offs
  • Only affects print mode; interactive mode is unaffected

1.6 Git Worktree Status Detection

Section titled “1.6 Git Worktree Status Detection”

What changed: New workspace.git_worktree field in the status line JSON.

Background: Git worktrees allow multiple working directories for the same repository, commonly used for parallel development/code review. Claude Code previously couldn’t distinguish between the main workspace and linked worktrees, potentially causing path confusion.

Use cases:

  • Using worktrees to handle multiple PRs in parallel
  • Correctly identifying context when running Claude Code in a worktree
  • Custom status line scripts adjusting behavior based on worktree status

Notes: 2.1.97 initially added this field; 2.1.98 ensures it’s correctly set in all scenarios.

1.7 OTEL Tracing — TRACEPARENT Propagation

Section titled “1.7 OTEL Tracing — TRACEPARENT Propagation”

What changed: Bash subprocesses now automatically inherit the W3C TRACEPARENT environment variable.

Background: When OpenTelemetry tracing was enabled, subprocess spans couldn’t properly attach to Claude Code’s trace tree, causing broken distributed traces.

Use cases:

  • Enterprise observability platform integration (Datadog, Honeycomb, Jaeger)
  • Debugging cross-process performance bottlenecks
  • Auditing all subprocess call chains triggered by Claude Code

1.8 LSP clientInfo Identification

Section titled “1.8 LSP clientInfo Identification”

What changed: Claude Code now identifies itself through the clientInfo field in LSP initialize requests.

Background: Language servers (LSP) couldn’t distinguish between requests from Claude Code and other editors, making it difficult to apply targeted optimizations or debugging.

Use cases:

  • LSP servers adjusting behavior based on client type
  • Quickly identifying the source when debugging LSP interaction issues

II. Security Fixes (Critical)

Section titled “II. Security Fixes (Critical)”

This release fixes multiple serious permission bypass vulnerabilities — the most critical part of this update.

2.1 Bash Tool Backslash Escape Bypass (Critical)

Section titled “2.1 Bash Tool Backslash Escape Bypass (Critical)”

Issue: Backslash-escaped flags could be auto-approved as “read-only” operations while actually executing arbitrary code.

Impact: An attacker (or malicious prompt) could craft commands with backslashes to bypass permission checks and execute dangerous operations in auto mode.

Fix: Escape characters are now normalized before permission matching.

2.2 Compound Command Bypass of Forced Permission Prompts

Section titled “2.2 Compound Command Bypass of Forced Permission Prompts”

Issue: Compound commands using pipes, &&, ;, etc. could bypass security checks in both auto and bypass-permissions modes.

Impact: Even with strict permission rules configured, dangerous parts of compound commands could be silently executed.

2.3 Environment Variable Prefix Bypass

Section titled “2.3 Environment Variable Prefix Bypass”

Issue: Commands in the format ENV_VAR=value dangerous_command would not trigger a permission prompt if ENV_VAR wasn’t on the known safe list.

Fix: Only known safe variables like LANG, TZ, NO_COLOR are now exempt from prompting.

2.4 /dev/tcp and /dev/udp Redirects

Section titled “2.4 /dev/tcp and /dev/udp Redirects”

Issue: Redirects to /dev/tcp/... or /dev/udp/... were automatically allowed and could be used for data exfiltration.

Fix: Such redirects now force a permission prompt.

2.5 Other Permission-Related Fixes

Section titled “2.5 Other Permission-Related Fixes”
  • --dangerously-skip-permissions silently downgraded to accept-edits after writing to protected paths
  • Admin-removed managed-settings rules remained effective until restart
  • additionalDirectories changes didn’t take effect in real time
  • Wildcard rules like Bash(cmd:*) didn’t match commands with extra spaces
  • Deny rules were downgraded in piped commands containing cd
  • grep -f / rg -f reading files outside the working directory didn’t trigger a prompt
  • JS prototype property names (e.g., toString) caused settings.json to be ignored

Overall assessment: This is a comprehensive security audit fix. Users running auto mode or bypass-permissions should upgrade immediately.

Comparison with similar products:

  • Codex CLI: Uses Docker sandbox with a different permission model; these bypasses don’t apply
  • Gemini CLI: Simpler permissions system with a smaller attack surface but also fewer features

III. Stability and Experience Fixes

Section titled “III. Stability and Experience Fixes”

3.1 Streaming Responses and Retries

Section titled “3.1 Streaming Responses and Retries”
  • Streaming responses now fall back to non-streaming mode after timeout (instead of failing outright)
  • Exponential backoff fix for 429 retries: previously, small Retry-After values burned through all retries within 13 seconds
  • 2.1.97 initially fixed this issue; 2.1.98 further refines it

3.2 Comprehensive /resume Fixes

Section titled “3.2 Comprehensive /resume Fixes”
  • --resume <name> opened as non-editable
  • Filter refresh cleared search state
  • Empty list swallowed arrow keys
  • Cross-project expiration issues
  • Task status text replaced conversation summaries
  • Added project/worktree/branch name filter indicators

3.3 Terminal Compatibility

Section titled “3.3 Terminal Compatibility”
  • Uppercase letters converted to lowercase under kitty keyboard protocol (xterm, VS Code terminal)
  • macOS text replacement deleted trigger words
  • Full-screen mode MCP tool result hover crash
  • URL copy inserting line break spaces

3.4 MCP-Related

Section titled “3.4 MCP-Related”
  • OAuth authServerMetadataUrl not working during token refresh after restart
  • _meta["anthropic/maxResultSizeChars"] not bypassing the token persistence layer

3.5 Permissions System Real-Time Updates

Section titled “3.5 Permissions System Real-Time Updates”
  • permissions.additionalDirectories changes now take effect immediately
  • Removing a directory no longer incorrectly revokes a same-named directory passed via --add-dir
  • Managed-settings rules take effect immediately after removal

IV. Improvements

Section titled “IV. Improvements”

4.1 /agents Tab Layout

Section titled “4.1 /agents Tab Layout”

New Running tab showing active subagents; Library tab adds “Run agent” and “View instances” actions.

4.2 Vim Mode Enhancements

Section titled “4.2 Vim Mode Enhancements”

NORMAL mode j/k navigates history, selecting the footer pill when reaching input boundaries.

4.3 Smarter Accept Edits Mode

Section titled “4.3 Smarter Accept Edits Mode”

Filesystem commands with safe environment variable prefixes or process wrappers (e.g., LANG=C rm foo, timeout 5 mkdir out) are now auto-approved.

4.4 Hook Error Diagnostics

Section titled “4.4 Hook Error Diagnostics”

Hook errors in transcripts now include the first line of stderr, enabling self-diagnosis without --debug.

4.5 DISABLE_COMPACT Refinements

Section titled “4.5 DISABLE_COMPACT Refinements”

When DISABLE_COMPACT is set, /compact prompts no longer appear, and CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_CONTEXT_TOKENS correctly respects this setting.

Vertex AI wizard, Perforce support, PID isolation, OTEL tracing — nearly all new features in 2.1.98 target enterprise users. Claude Code is evolving from a “developer tool” into an “enterprise development platform.”

Fixing 10+ permission bypass issues at once indicates Anthropic conducted a systematic security audit. This is a necessary step for AI coding tools moving into production environments. Expect continued tightening of the permission model in future releases.

From AWS Bedrock to GCP Vertex AI, Claude Code is building a multi-cloud support matrix. Compared to Codex CLI (OpenAI only) and Gemini CLI (Google only), this is a unique competitive advantage.

OpenClaw 2026.4.9 Deep Analysis: Memory Governance, Security Tightening, and Plugin-Driven Auth

Apr 9, 2026
Vibe Sparking

OpenClaw 2026.4.9 Deep Analysis

Section titled “OpenClaw 2026.4.9 Deep Analysis”

Generated: 2026-04-09 12:30 CST

Overall take

Section titled “Overall take”

OpenClaw 2026.4.9 is not a flashy feature release. It is a product-grade consolidation release that pushes Memory, Auth, Security, and cross-platform consistency forward in one move.

If 2026.4.8 was about getting the system running and smoothing deployment, then 2026.4.9 is about runtime trustworthiness, memory governance, plugin extensibility, and release engineering.

This release can be grouped into six major themes:

  1. Memory and Dreaming move from experimental capability to traceable, replayable, governable infrastructure
  2. Security tightens further, especially around post-interaction safety checks, untrusted input isolation, and remote text pretending to be trusted system content
  3. Provider and Auth logic continue moving out of hard-coded core paths and into plugin-declared capabilities
  4. QA evolves from “does it work” toward comparing character, tone, and model behavior in parallel
  5. Cross-platform engineering gets stronger, especially across iOS, Android, Windows, and package integrity
  6. Many small routing, reply, and streaming bugs were fixed, which is a classic sign of a system entering the real-world reliability phase

In one sentence:

The value of 2026.4.9 is not that OpenClaw can do dramatically more, but that it looks more like a long-term operable, auditable, and safely extensible agent runtime.

Memory becomes a cognition system

Section titled “Memory becomes a cognition system”

The most important product signal in this release is the continued evolution of Memory and Dreaming.

Grounded REM backfill, historical REM harnesses, diary commit/reset, durable fact extraction, and live short-term promotion all point in the same direction: OpenClaw is no longer treating memory as a passive archive. It is treating memory as a managed cognitive substrate.

That matters because older agent memory systems usually had a structural split:

  • new conversations entered memory pipelines,
  • old daily logs stayed as dead files,
  • upgraded extraction logic could not replay historical notes cleanly,
  • and short-term versus long-term memory slowly diverged.

This release addresses that directly. Historical daily notes can be replayed into a newer memory pipeline, producing dream-layer summaries, durable facts, and promotion candidates. That turns old notes from static archives into reprocessable cognition inputs.

At the same time, this is a risky path. Historical contamination, duplicate fact promotion, incorrect attribution, and memory noise are real dangers. The fact that OpenClaw added grounded lanes, traceability, reset paths, and extraction hardening alongside the feature is a very good sign. It suggests the authors understand that this is a high-risk write path into the agent’s long-term mind.

Control UI becomes an observability console

Section titled “Control UI becomes an observability console”

The companion change is just as important: these memory and dreaming capabilities are being surfaced in a UI people can inspect and operate.

That matters because memory systems are often not limited by capability, but by explainability. Users need to see:

  • what was remembered,
  • why it was remembered,
  • what is staged versus grounded versus promoted,
  • where a durable fact came from,
  • and how to reset a questionable backfill run.

A structured diary view, timeline navigation, traceable summaries, grounded scene lanes, and backfill controls move OpenClaw closer to a true runtime observability console. It becomes much easier to debug memory behavior, audit provenance, and understand how an agent’s beliefs were formed.

This likely points toward future features such as memory lineage graphs, durable fact approval flows, confidence scores, and conflict resolution between competing facts.

QA becomes personality engineering

Section titled “QA becomes personality engineering”

The QA and Lab work is another clear signal.

Character-vibes evaluation reports, model selection tools, and parallel runs show that OpenClaw is no longer satisfied with “the model works.” It is starting to evaluate whether a model behaves like the intended agent.

That is a major shift. In agent products, quality is not just factual correctness anymore. It also includes:

  • whether the tone is too verbose,
  • whether the personality drifts after a prompt change,
  • whether a fallback model still feels like the same agent,
  • whether a system prompt produces the right operational style.

This is the beginning of personality engineering as a first-class QA discipline.

Provider/Auth becomes more plugin-native

Section titled “Provider/Auth becomes more plugin-native”

providerAuthAliases is one of the most strategically important architecture changes in this release.

It lets provider manifests declare shared authentication aliases so that related provider variants can reuse env vars, auth profiles, config-backed auth, and onboarding choices without hard-coding all of that into the core.

That is exactly the right direction for a growing plugin ecosystem. Otherwise the core becomes bloated with one-off provider rules.

But it also introduces real trust-boundary concerns, including alias collisions, untrusted plugins pretending to be bundled providers, and the risk of routing operator secrets into the wrong plugin tier. The presence of collision fixes and trust filtering around onboarding confirms that OpenClaw is trying to improve extensibility without relaxing security boundaries.

Security is maturing into zero-trust runtime discipline

Section titled “Security is maturing into zero-trust runtime discipline”

The most important fixes in this release are security-related.

Post-interaction blocked-destination safety checks

Section titled “Post-interaction blocked-destination safety checks”

This is one of the most important fixes in the release because it closes a classic browser automation gap.

A browser may start from a safe URL, but after a click, script evaluation, hook-triggered action, or batched navigation, it might be redirected toward an internal or blocked destination. If safety checks happen only at the initial request, SSRF-style bypasses become possible.

Re-running blocked-destination checks after interaction-driven navigations is exactly the kind of fix a mature agent browser needs.

Blocking runtime-control env vars from untrusted workspace .env

Section titled “Blocking runtime-control env vars from untrusted workspace .env”

This is another high-value hardening fix.

If an untrusted workspace .env can override runtime control variables, browser control endpoints, or skip-server behavior, then simply opening a repository can silently alter how the agent runtime behaves. That is a supply-chain style risk. Downgrading trust in workspace .env files is the correct move.

Sanitizing remote node exec summaries as untrusted system events

Section titled “Sanitizing remote node exec summaries as untrusted system events”

This closes another critical trust boundary.

In a multi-node environment, remote command output should never be treated as inherently trusted. If remote summaries can appear as if they were genuine system messages, they can become prompt-injection carriers. Sanitizing those summaries as untrusted events is essential once the platform supports remote orchestration.

Auth-choice collisions in plugin onboarding

Section titled “Auth-choice collisions in plugin onboarding”

This is ecosystem security work. If an untrusted plugin can register an onboarding auth choice that looks like an official one, it may be able to confuse setup flows or intercept credentials. Namespace and trust-tier isolation are mandatory once plugin onboarding becomes sophisticated.

Reliability fixes matter too

Section titled “Reliability fixes matter too”

A large part of the release is made of smaller fixes across routing, replies, streaming, Android pairing, Slack, Matrix, npm packaging, SDK exports, Windows updates, and model/provider handling.

Individually, these may look minor. Collectively, they are the signature of a platform that is being used heavily in the real world.

These fixes suggest OpenClaw is doing the hard work of separating internal control signals from user-visible output, preserving route correctness across sessions, keeping package artifacts installable, and making multi-surface behavior feel consistent.

Strategic trajectory

Section titled “Strategic trajectory”

This release fits four longer trends:

1. Security is moving from big-hole patching to boundary refinement

Section titled “1. Security is moving from big-hole patching to boundary refinement”

The system is no longer only fixing dramatic holes. It is now hardening window seams: post-click navigation checks, remote event sanitization, env-var trust boundaries, onboarding namespace collisions, and package audit discipline.

2. Memory is moving from storage to cognition

Section titled “2. Memory is moving from storage to cognition”

The strongest message in this release is this:

OpenClaw no longer treats memory as an attachment. It is building memory into the substrate of agent cognition.

3. Provider/Auth is moving from core special-casing to manifest-driven declarations

Section titled “3. Provider/Auth is moving from core special-casing to manifest-driven declarations”

That means fewer hard-coded provider exceptions and more provider-declared capabilities, auth flows, and public contracts.

4. Control UI is becoming a true runtime observability layer

Section titled “4. Control UI is becoming a true runtime observability layer”

It is no longer just a management console. It is becoming a place to inspect memory traces, route behavior, model selection correctness, and operational state.

Competitive positioning

Section titled “Competitive positioning”

Compared with lighter runtimes, OpenClaw is clearly choosing the heavy-platform path.

  • Against NanoClaw, it trades simplicity for breadth and platform depth.
  • Against Nanobot, it looks more like a full operating platform than a hackable lightweight runtime.
  • Against IronClaw, it is absorbing more zero-trust thinking without becoming purely security-first.
  • Against PicoClaw, it is solving scale and complexity rather than minimal footprint.
  • Against ZeroClaw, it is less architecturally pure but stronger in real-world integration and product surface.

Final conclusion

Section titled “Final conclusion”

OpenClaw 2026.4.9 is a release that thickens the platform foundation.

Its real value is not in any single changelog item, but in the fact that several strategic directions move forward together:

  • memory becomes more like a cognition system
  • security becomes more like a zero-trust runtime discipline
  • provider/auth becomes more like a plugin protocol
  • QA becomes more like personality engineering
  • the Control UI becomes more like an observability center

If lighter competitors win by being small, fast, and clean, then OpenClaw is betting on something harder:

not just being an agent that can run, but being an agent platform that can be operated, audited, governed, and safely extended over time.

OpenClaw 2026.4.9-beta.1 Deep Dive: Memory Backfill, Security Hardening, and Delivery Reliability

Apr 9, 2026
Vibe Sparking

OpenClaw 2026.4.9-beta.1 Deep Dive: Memory Backfill, Security Hardening, and Delivery Reliability

Section titled “OpenClaw 2026.4.9-beta.1 Deep Dive: Memory Backfill, Security Hardening, and Delivery Reliability”

1. The short version: what this release is really doing

Section titled “1. The short version: what this release is really doing”

OpenClaw 2026.4.9-beta.1 is not mainly about adding flashy features. It is continuing to close five major loops:

  1. Memory/Dreaming is evolving from an experimental feature into a replayable, auditable, operable cognition pipeline
  2. Security boundaries are getting harder, especially around workspace, browser, remote node, and plugin injection
  3. Multi-channel messaging is getting more precise, reducing duplicate replies, route drift, and internal control-token leaks
  4. Plugin and provider boundaries are becoming more stable, moving toward a real platform SDK
  5. QA, Control UI, and Mobile are getting more usable operationally, not just more feature-rich

If you run multi-instance OpenClaw environments, the most important changes in this beta are:

  • dreaming backfill and grounded lanes
  • browser SSRF fixes
  • dotenv and workspace plugin security patches
  • remote node exec event trust boundaries
  • sessions routing, reply, NO_REPLY, Slack, Matrix, and other delivery-correctness fixes
  • provider-auth aliases and plugin SDK cleanup

2. Overall trajectory

Section titled “2. Overall trajectory”

Compared with recent versions, this beta makes it even clearer that OpenClaw is moving from:

  • “an agent runtime that can chat”

into:

  • an agent OS with memory, orchestration, auditability, and safety boundaries

That direction is consistent with what we already saw around 2026.4.2 and 2026.4.5.

3. Detailed analysis by theme

Section titled “3. Detailed analysis by theme”

A. Memory / Dreaming

Section titled “A. Memory / Dreaming”

1) Memory/dreaming: grounded REM backfill lane

Section titled “1) Memory/dreaming: grounded REM backfill lane”

The underlying problem

Older agent memory systems usually run into the same issues:

  • historical daily notes exist on disk, but never flow back into long-term memory
  • old and new memory paths diverge into two memory stacks
  • durable-fact extraction is noisy
  • historical replay is hard to trace or roll back

What this release is solving

The biggest improvement here is this:

old daily notes can finally be replayed into Dreams and durable memory in a grounded way, without maintaining a second memory stack.

In other words, historical notes are being absorbed into the same promotion pipeline as current memory.

Typical use cases

  1. Backfilling historical memory into an old workspace
  2. Rebuilding Dreams and durable facts after migrating an instance
  3. Extracting stable operational knowledge from historical logs

Example

Imagine a manager agent whose daily notes repeatedly mention things like:

  • after a tunnel IP change, known_hosts must be updated
  • some providers time out under specific transports
  • some reply fallbacks duplicate messages on certain channels

The ideal outcome of dreaming backfill is that these repeated observations become durable facts instead of staying buried in daily notes forever.

Cautions

  • backfill is high value, but also high risk
  • it can over-promote noisy or outdated information
  • old mistakes can become durable truths
  • source attribution can become messy if you do not inspect it carefully

A practical recommendation is to backfill in smaller batches, enable tracing, and manually review durable facts.

Relation to earlier releases

  • 2026.4.2 and 2026.4.5 looked like foundation work for dreaming and promotion
  • 2026.4.9-beta.1 starts filling in historical replay, grounded lanes, commit/reset, and traceability

2) Control UI/dreaming: structured diary view and grounded Scene lane

Section titled “2) Control UI/dreaming: structured diary view and grounded Scene lane”

The underlying problem

If dreaming only exists in the background with no UI:

  • operators cannot see what the system remembered
  • they cannot tell where a promotion came from
  • mistakes cannot be reset or backfilled cleanly
  • “dreaming” turns into a black box

What this release adds

The Control UI now includes:

  • a structured diary view
  • timeline navigation
  • backfill/reset controls
  • traceable dreaming summaries
  • a grounded Scene lane
  • promotion hints
  • safe clear-grounded operations

That matters because memory is no longer just files and logs. It is becoming a visual cognition-operations interface.

Use cases

  • auditing dreaming results
  • tracing a durable fact back to a specific day
  • resetting incorrect promotions
  • cleaning grounded signals in staged backfill passes

Caution

promotion hints are still hints, not truth. The existence of safe clear-grounded also tells you the system expects staged signals to become dirty sometimes.

3) Memory/dreaming hardening and heartbeat token support

Section titled “3) Memory/dreaming hardening and heartbeat token support”

The underlying problem

Backfill is most fragile when:

  • the path is wrong
  • symlinks contaminate the read path
  • source-day tags get lost
  • diary titles are inconsistent
  • claim splitting is too aggressive
  • runtime wrappers swallow heartbeat tokens and dreaming never triggers

Why this matters

This is a sign that the project is moving from “can the feature work” to “is the input trustworthy, is metadata stable, and can we trace the result.”

B. QA / Lab / Live behavior

Section titled “B. QA / Lab / Live behavior”

4) QA/lab: character-vibes evaluation reports

Section titled “4) QA/lab: character-vibes evaluation reports”

The underlying problem

Traditional QA usually focuses on:

  • whether a feature works
  • whether tool calls succeed
  • whether output errors out

But agent products also need to test something much harder:

  • whether style stays consistent
  • whether persona drifts
  • how different models feel under the same agent
  • which candidate model actually matches the intended character

What this release changes

It adds:

  • character-vibes evaluation reports
  • model selection
  • parallel runs

That means QA is expanding from functional correctness into behavioral and stylistic consistency.

Use cases

  • comparing multiple models under the same persona
  • checking whether an upgrade makes the agent too verbose, too cold, or too reckless
  • doing A/B model selection

Caution

vibes evaluation does not replace functional QA. Parallel runs are good for evaluation, not for live tasks with external side effects.

5) QA/live auth: fail fast on auth/runtime failures

Section titled “5) QA/live auth: fail fast on auth/runtime failures”

The underlying problem

The most annoying part of live QA is not failure itself, but ambiguous failure:

  • an auth problem looks like a timeout
  • missing credentials just hang
  • runtime failures get swallowed

Why this matters

This improves error quality. Auth and runtime failures become actionable failures instead of vague timeouts.

C. Plugins / SDK / Provider auth

Section titled “C. Plugins / SDK / Provider auth”

6) Plugins/provider-auth: providerAuthAliases

Section titled “6) Plugins/provider-auth: providerAuthAliases”

The underlying problem

Once your provider ecosystem gets bigger, you usually end up with:

  • one provider having multiple variants
  • variants that should share env vars or auth profiles
  • growing maintenance cost because the core has to special-case everything

What this release does

It lets a provider manifest declare providerAuthAliases, so variants can share:

  • environment variables
  • auth profiles
  • config-backed auth
  • onboarding choices

without adding more hardcoded logic to the core.

Caution

Shared auth is convenient, but trust and capability boundaries still matter. Shared credentials do not mean identical behavior.

7) Plugins/onboarding auth choices collision fix

Section titled “7) Plugins/onboarding auth choices collision fix”

The underlying problem

If an untrusted plugin can impersonate a bundled provider’s auth-choice ID, it might:

  • hijack onboarding flows
  • get closer to operator secrets
  • interfere with non-interactive install behavior

Why this matters

This is an important supply-chain and plugin trust-boundary fix.

8) Plugin SDK export cleanup, contracts, and command-status split

Section titled “8) Plugin SDK export cleanup, contracts, and command-status split”

The underlying problem

Early SDKs often suffer from:

  • incomplete public APIs, forcing developers into private imports
  • test helpers leaking into production barrels
  • auth-only plugins pulling in too much status/context machinery

What this release is doing

  • exporting a real channel plugin base
  • exporting the web-search config contract
  • isolating test-only helpers from production code
  • adding a lightweight openclaw/plugin-sdk/command-status subpath

D. Security

Section titled “D. Security”

9) Browser/security: interaction-driven navigation re-check

Section titled “9) Browser/security: interaction-driven navigation re-check”

The underlying problem

SSRF defenses often catch direct access to blocked URLs, but miss the more subtle flow:

  1. open a safe page
  2. navigate through click/evaluate/hook/batched actions to a dangerous destination
  3. never re-run the safety checks after the navigation

What this release fixes

It re-runs blocked-destination safety checks for interaction-driven main-frame navigation.

Caution

Some previously working browser automations may now be blocked. That is the correct kind of breaking change.

10) Security/dotenv: block runtime-control env vars from untrusted workspace .env

Section titled “10) Security/dotenv: block runtime-control env vars from untrusted workspace .env”

The underlying problem

If a workspace .env can change runtime behavior, it opens a dangerous local injection surface:

  • browser-control overrides
  • skip-server switches
  • runtime-control env vars
  • URL-style override specifiers

Why this matters

This is a key local supply-chain defense. It makes the trust boundary explicit:

workspace config is not operator config, and an untrusted repo must not control the runtime control plane

11) Gateway/node exec events: mark as untrusted and sanitize

Section titled “11) Gateway/node exec events: mark as untrusted and sanitize”

The underlying problem

If exec event summaries coming from remote nodes are treated as trusted system events, they can become a prompt-injection path via:

  • fake System: content
  • malicious summaries
  • contamination of later turns

What this release changes

Those remote exec summaries are now treated as untrusted system events and sanitized consistently.

12) Security/dependency audit: basic-ftp and Hono bumps

Section titled “12) Security/dependency audit: basic-ftp and Hono bumps”

Why this matters

  • basic-ftp 5.2.1 closes a CRLF command-injection issue
  • Hono and @hono/node-server upgrades improve web-runtime security and compatibility

E. Gateway / Sessions / Chat delivery correctness

Section titled “E. Gateway / Sessions / Chat delivery correctness”

13) Reply/doctor improvements

Section titled “13) Reply/doctor improvements”

The underlying problem

Asynchronous reply paths often fail in messy ways:

  • they use stale runtime snapshots
  • SecretRef resolution happens in the wrong context
  • expired OAuth looks like a generic failure
  • doctor output does not tell you how to re-authenticate

Why this matters

Queued replies get aligned more closely with the current runtime, and re-auth instructions become much more actionable.

14) Control UI: stale session-history reload guard

Section titled “14) Control UI: stale session-history reload guard”

The underlying problem

Fast session switching often creates async race conditions where:

  • the left panel selects session A
  • the right panel renders transcript B

15) Gateway/chat: suppress ANNOUNCE_SKIP / REPLY_SKIP leaks

Section titled “15) Gateway/chat: suppress ANNOUNCE_SKIP / REPLY_SKIP leaks”

The underlying problem

Internal control tokens should never leak into the user-visible UI.

16) Auto-reply/NO_REPLY: strip glued leading NO_REPLY tokens

Section titled “16) Auto-reply/NO_REPLY: strip glued leading NO_REPLY tokens”

The underlying problem

If a silent sentinel token gets glued to a normal reply, it leaks into the user interface.

17) Sessions/routing: preserve established external routes

Section titled “17) Sessions/routing: preserve established external routes”

The underlying problem

If sessions_send follow-ups steal existing external routes, replies can end up in the wrong channel.

18) Gateway/sessions: clear auto-fallback-pinned model overrides on /reset and /new

Section titled “18) Gateway/sessions: clear auto-fallback-pinned model overrides on /reset and /new”

The underlying problem

The system needs to distinguish between:

  1. explicit user model overrides
  2. automatically pinned fallback models

Otherwise stale model state survives resets unexpectedly.

19) Slack/media, Slack/ACP, and Slack partial streaming

Section titled “19) Slack/media, Slack/ACP, and Slack partial streaming”

Shared background

Channel delivery is not just about “message sent.” It also needs to handle previews, fallbacks, redirects, block rendering, and deduplication of partially streamed messages.

20) Matrix/gateway and Matrix/doctor

Section titled “20) Matrix/gateway and Matrix/doctor”

The underlying problem

  • sync may not be ready even though startup looks successful
  • background handler crashes can destabilize the whole gateway
  • schema changes can leave doctor unable to migrate old config cleanly

21) QQBot/media-tags

Section titled “21) QQBot/media-tags”

The underlying problem

Upstream message formats are often messy:

  • HTML entity angle brackets
  • slashes in URL-like attrs
  • self-closing tags

F. Mobile

Section titled “F. Mobile”

22) Android/pairing and Android/manual connect

Section titled “22) Android/pairing and Android/manual connect”

The underlying problem

Mobile pairing becomes painful when a single stale setup state poisons every later attempt.

This set of fixes focuses on:

  • cleaning stale setup-code auth
  • using fresh pairing bootstrap
  • preferring stored device tokens after bootstrap
  • pausing auto-retry in background
  • defaulting TLS manual endpoints to port 443 when the port is omitted

23) iOS: explicit CalVer pinning

Section titled “23) iOS: explicit CalVer pinning”

The underlying problem

TestFlight and release trains often suffer from:

  • short version vs build number confusion
  • iOS release cadence drifting from gateway release cadence
  • short-version churn during rapid testing

G. Providers / Auth / Agents

Section titled “G. Providers / Auth / Agents”

24) Providers/OpenAI: default reasoning set to high

Section titled “24) Providers/OpenAI: default reasoning set to high”

The underlying problem

If the default reasoning effort differs across transports, users get inconsistent behavior under what feels like the same configuration.

Caution

  • cost and latency may increase
  • answer quality and stability may improve

25) Providers/Ollama: native API path supports thinking output

Section titled “25) Providers/Ollama: native API path supports thinking output”

The underlying problem

Local-model users increasingly care about visible thinking traces, but native api: "ollama" paths often lag behind in support.

26) Auth/profiles: persist explicit upserts locally

Section titled “26) Auth/profiles: persist explicit upserts locally”

The underlying problem

When auth-profile changes depend on external CLI sync to become durable, local state can stay stale or get overwritten.

27) Agents/timeouts

Section titled “27) Agents/timeouts”

The underlying problem

If timeout behavior is not unified, users see:

  • defaults that do not propagate to idle watchdogs
  • cron runs dying unexpectedly from idle limits
  • inconsistent error fields

28) Agents/failover: Z.ai code classification

Section titled “28) Agents/failover: Z.ai code classification”

The underlying problem

If vendor-specific error codes are classified incorrectly, failover behavior becomes unreliable.

29) Codex CLI: pass system prompt via model_instructions_file

Section titled “29) Codex CLI: pass system prompt via model_instructions_file”

The underlying problem

If Codex CLI sessions and Claude CLI sessions do not receive equivalent system prompts, their behavior can diverge in confusing ways.

H. Packaging / Build / Windows

Section titled “H. Packaging / Build / Windows”

30) npm packaging hardening

Section titled “30) npm packaging hardening”

The underlying problem

Many dependency issues only appear in packed installs that no longer rely on repository node_modules layouts.

31) Windows/update: add heap headroom

Section titled “31) Windows/update: add heap headroom”

The underlying problem

Windows dev updates and pnpm build preflight paths often fail because the default Node heap is too small.

4. Comparison with similar open-source products

5. Upgrade notes and validation priorities

Section titled “5. Upgrade notes and validation priorities”

Production cautions

Section titled “Production cautions”
  1. do not enable dreaming backfill at full scale immediately
  2. .env security tightening may break older workflows
  3. stronger browser SSRF protections may block old automations

Recommended validation order for cluster managers

    • remote node exec event sanitization
  2. Session and channel correctness
    • sessions_send route preservation
    • Slack fallback and partial streaming
    • Matrix startup and restart behavior
    • NO_REPLY / ANNOUNCE_SKIP leakage
  3. Memory and dreaming
    • historical backfill
    • grounded diary traceability
    • heartbeat token integration
  4. Providers and plugins
    • providerAuthAliases
    • local auth-profile persistence
    • plugin SDK exports
  5. Mobile and packaging
    • Android pairing
    • iOS version pinning
    • packed-install smoke tests

6. Where this is heading next

Section titled “6. Where this is heading next”
  1. dreaming will keep evolving into a formal knowledge-operations system
  2. security work will continue shifting from external attack surfaces to local and internal trust boundaries
  3. channels will increasingly look like a message-dispatch operating system
  4. the plugin platform will become more manifest-first and keep thinning the core
  5. QA will become more behavior-centric
  6. OpenClaw will look more and more like an agent OS rather than a bot framework

7. Final judgment

Section titled “7. Final judgment”

2026.4.9-beta.1 is a beta focused on platform maturation, safety boundaries, and cognition infrastructure.

In one sentence:

It is not aggressively adding surface-level features. It is continuing to push OpenClaw toward production-grade foundations across memory, safety, plugin architecture, channel delivery, and operational visibility.

OpenClaw 2026.4.7 Bug Fixes Deep Analysis

Apr 8, 2026
Vibe Sparking

This document provides a deep analysis of all 71 bug fixes in the OpenClaw 2026.4.7 release.

1. CLI/infer: Align Inference Behavior with Actual Runtime Execution

Section titled “1. CLI/infer: Align Inference Behavior with Actual Runtime Execution”

Fix Summary

Section titled “Fix Summary”

Fixed multiple inconsistencies between openclaw infer CLI command and the actual runtime, including TTS overrides, profile-aware gateway TTS preferences, transcription prompt/language overrides, image output MIME/extension mismatch, web-search fallback, and agent vs CLI web-search behavior drift.

Background

Section titled “Background”

openclaw infer as a standalone CLI inference command should produce results identical to the agent runtime. However, as features evolved, the two paths diverged: TTS configuration didn’t read profile-level preferences, transcription ignored user-specified prompt and language parameters, image generation MIME types didn’t match file extensions (e.g., returning PNG data but labeling as .jpg), and web-search had fallback logic in the agent but not in CLI. The root cause was insufficient code sharing between infer and agent paths.

Impact

Section titled “Impact”
  • Voice generated via openclaw infer --tts differed from agent conversations
  • Image file extensions didn’t match actual content, causing viewer failures
  • Web-search results differed between CLI and agent, breaking automation scripts

2. Plugins/media: Merge Capability Plugin IDs into Allowlist

Section titled “2. Plugins/media: Merge Capability Plugin IDs into Allowlist”

Fix Summary

Section titled “Fix Summary”

When plugins.allow is set, the capability fallback logic now merges built-in capability plugin IDs into the allow list, so OpenAI-compatible STT and other media providers load without explicitly declaring openai in plugins.allow. (#62205)

Background

Section titled “Background”

OpenClaw’s plugin security model lets users restrict loadable plugins via plugins.allow. But built-in “capability plugins” (like STT providers) are core platform features, not third-party plugins. The previous implementation only merged IDs from plugins.entries, missing built-in capability plugin IDs.

Turning the Skill Vetter Guide into a Skill: A Full Practice from Creation to Publishing and Real Use

Apr 5, 2026
Vibe Sparking

Turning the Skill Vetter Guide into a Skill: A Full Practice from Creation to Publishing and Real Use

Section titled “Turning the Skill Vetter Guide into a Skill: A Full Practice from Creation to Publishing and Real Use”

Date: 2026-04-05

Today I did something that feels very OpenClaw in spirit: instead of writing a documentation file just for myself, I took a complete body of material around Skill Vetter installation, configuration, usage, SOPs, workflows, and best practices and packaged it into a skill that other OpenClaw users can directly reuse — skill-vetter-guide.

Repository: https://github.com/vs-agent-skills/skill-vetter-guide

On the surface, this looks like “writing docs.” In reality, it is a layer of reusable operational abstraction: turning procedures that previously lived in chat history, personal experience, and scattered notes into a skill that an OpenClaw agent can recognize, read, execute, and reuse.

This is not “just wrapping one more layer around it.” It lowers friction, improves consistency, and reduces mistakes.

1. The Starting Point: The Documentation Existed, but It Wasn’t Usable Enough

Section titled “1. The Starting Point: The Documentation Existed, but It Wasn’t Usable Enough”

The starting point was simple.

A long-form guide about Skill Vetter already existed. It covered:

  • what Skill Vetter is
  • where it should be installed
  • why third-party skills must be reviewed before installation
  • what to inspect during a review
  • common red flags
  • how to classify risk
  • how to produce a standard vetting report
  • how to run periodic audits
  • how to write “review before install” into AGENTS.md
  • and prompt templates that OpenClaw can directly use

That kind of document is useful for humans, but it has an obvious limitation:

It was still mainly written for people to read, not for agents to directly use.

In other words, the information existed, but the usage flow was still too manual:

  1. Find the document
  2. Read it yourself
  3. Understand it yourself
  4. Copy a prompt block yourself
  5. Adapt it yourself
  6. Send it to another OpenClaw yourself

That flow is not impossible, but it is noisy and easy to distort.

Especially when the goal is not just “something I might refer back to later,” but rather:

  • sharing it with other OpenClaw users
  • letting other agents reuse it consistently
  • lowering the barrier to using Skill Vetter
  • making “vet first, install later” a standard action

At that point, it should not stop at the documentation layer.

It should become a skill.

2. Why Turn SOPs, Workflows, and Best Practices into a Skill

Section titled “2. Why Turn SOPs, Workflows, and Best Practices into a Skill”

This is the core of the whole exercise.

A lot of people write SOPs and end up with a “knowledge article.” But in OpenClaw, the more effective move is often this:

Turn knowledge into a skill, and turn experience into something triggerable.

2.1 A Skill Is Closer to Executable Knowledge Than an Article

Section titled “2.1 A Skill Is Closer to Executable Knowledge Than an Article”

An article explains a problem. A skill intervenes when the problem actually appears.

An article, no matter how complete, is still static. A skill can be matched, loaded, and applied by the agent when a relevant task shows up.

For example:

  • the user says “help me install this third-party skill”
  • the agent recognizes it as a skill-installation task
  • the agent reads skill-vetter-guide
  • it runs the agreed safety review flow first
  • then it decides whether installation is acceptable

At that point, the SOP is no longer “do you remember to use it?” It becomes “will the system use it automatically?”

That is a huge difference.

2.2 A Skill Turns Tacit Experience into Explicit Rules

Section titled “2.2 A Skill Turns Tacit Experience into Explicit Rules”

A lot of best practices normally live only in experienced users’ heads, for example:

  • do not review only SKILL.md; review all files
  • be cautious around curl, wget, and external fetches
  • reading ~/.ssh, ~/.aws, or MEMORY.md is high risk by default
  • eval, exec, and base64 obfuscation deserve special scrutiny
  • HIGH and EXTREME risks require human confirmation
  • keep an audit trail after installation

If these rules exist only in chat, they disappear in context churn. If they exist only in a long article, they are easy to skip.

Once they are written into a skill, though, they become reusable, portable, easy to copy across instances, easy to share for direct use, and capable of forming consistent habits.

That is experience productized.

2.3 Skills Naturally Fit Cross-Instance and Cross-User Sharing

Section titled “2.3 Skills Naturally Fit Cross-Instance and Cross-User Sharing”

One major reality of OpenClaw is that agents and instances are often distributed:

  • different machines
  • different workspaces
  • different agent personas
  • different channels
  • different maintainers

If everyone relies on handwritten SOPs and custom prompt rewrites, the result will eventually be version drift, inconsistent rules, missed reviews, and repeated labor.

Once it becomes a skill, the sharing model becomes much cleaner: one directory, one file structure, one repository, and one format the agent can recognize.

2.4 A Skill Lowers the Barrier to Usage, Not the Bar for Safety

Section titled “2.4 A Skill Lowers the Barrier to Usage, Not the Bar for Safety”

The biggest problem in many safety workflows is not conceptual difficulty. It is procedural fragmentation.

Skill Vetter itself is not mysterious. It is a straightforward safety review logic:

  • inspect the source
  • inspect the code
  • inspect the permissions
  • inspect the risks
  • make a conclusion

Putting those answers into a skill means users no longer have to reconstruct the entire context from scratch every time.

not lowering the standard, but lowering the friction required to enter the standard process.

3. How It Was Built

Section titled “3. How It Was Built”

The process roughly unfolded in four steps: start from a complete guide, reshape it into a skill structure, unify around English first and then add Chinese, and finally publish it so it becomes something truly shareable.

3.1 Start with a Complete Source Guide

Section titled “3.1 Start with a Complete Source Guide”

The first step was to write a sufficiently complete guide for Skill Vetter itself. That source material covered its positioning, recommended install path, pre-install vetting SOP, red-flag checklist, risk grading model, standard report template, audit suggestions, prompt templates, and recommended AGENTS.md rules.

3.2 Convert the Document into a Skill Structure

Section titled “3.2 Convert the Document into a Skill Structure”

The final shape included:

  • SKILL.md
  • references/report-template.md
  • references/audit-template.md
  • references/prompt-templates.md

The main file carries the principles and entry points. The reference files hold details and reusable templates.

3.3 Standardize on English First, Then Add Chinese

Section titled “3.3 Standardize on English First, Then Add Chinese”

To make the material more suitable for public sharing, the content was first normalized into an English-primary version. But English alone would not be enough for a large group of actual OpenClaw users, so a corresponding Chinese version was also added.

3.4 Publish It to GitHub So It Becomes a Real Shared Asset

Section titled “3.4 Publish It to GitHub So It Becomes a Real Shared Asset”

Only after publishing does it stop being “personal material” and become a shared asset. So the work was organized into an independent repository and published here:

https://github.com/vs-agent-skills/skill-vetter-guide

Along the way, the repository setup was also cleaned up: explicit Git identity, SSH key setup, SSH commit signing, and proper organization ownership.

4. What Problem This Skill Actually Solves

Section titled “4. What Problem This Skill Actually Solves”

4.1 It Solves “I Know I Should Review, but I Don’t Know How”

Section titled “4.1 It Solves “I Know I Should Review, but I Don’t Know How””

skill-vetter-guide turns the review process into a template: what files to inspect, what behaviors are dangerous, what counts as high risk, and how to produce a disciplined conclusion.

4.2 It Solves the Repetition of Explaining the Same Workflow Again and Again

Section titled “4.2 It Solves the Repetition of Explaining the Same Workflow Again and Again”

Without the skill, every explanation tends to repeat the same pieces: where to install it, how to use it, how to vet before install, how to write prompts, and how to audit afterward.

4.3 It Solves Inconsistent Standards Across Instances

Section titled “4.3 It Solves Inconsistent Standards Across Instances”

A shared skill helps unify SOPs, risk language, review templates, and audit outputs.

4.4 It Solves the Risk of Keeping Safety Rules Only in Someone’s Head

Section titled “4.4 It Solves the Risk of Keeping Safety Rules Only in Someone’s Head”

Writing them into a skill upgrades safety habits from personal memory into shared capability.

5. Why This Is More Valuable Than Publishing a Tutorial Alone

Section titled “5. Why This Is More Valuable Than Publishing a Tutorial Alone”

If you only publish an article, people get an explanation, a set of recommendations, and some prompt snippets. If you publish a skill, they get structured content, an agent-recognizable entry point, reusable templates, a consistent operating pattern, and a shared repository that can keep evolving.

For an agent-first system like OpenClaw, something the agent can directly use is often more valuable than something thoroughly written for humans.

6. Practical Use Cases: How It Can Be Used Going Forward

Section titled “6. Practical Use Cases: How It Can Be Used Going Forward”

Scenario 1: New Machine Bring-Up

Section titled “Scenario 1: New Machine Bring-Up”

When a fresh OpenClaw instance is being set up, the agent can install Skill Vetter first, read skill-vetter-guide, write “review before install” into AGENTS.md, and configure the audit flow afterward.

Section titled “Scenario 2: Reviewing a Third-Party Skill”

The next time a new skill appears, there is no need to improvise the language from scratch. Just tell the agent: vet it first, use Skill Vetter, follow the guide.

Scenario 3: Sharing OpenClaw Best Practices with Others

Section titled “Scenario 3: Sharing OpenClaw Best Practices with Others”

If someone asks how to install and manage third-party skills safely in OpenClaw, there is no longer a need for a long explanation. Just hand them the repository:

https://github.com/vs-agent-skills/skill-vetter-guide

Scenario 4: Acting as a Team-Wide Standard

Section titled “Scenario 4: Acting as a Team-Wide Standard”

If multiple people are maintaining OpenClaw within a team, skill-vetter-guide can act as a shared internal standard for what must be reviewed, what must be blocked, what counts as high risk, how reports should be written, and how audit traces should be kept.

7. The Bigger Meaning: Upgrading “Experience Documents” into “Distributable Capability”

Section titled “7. The Bigger Meaning: Upgrading “Experience Documents” into “Distributable Capability””

In OpenClaw, many high-value pieces of operational knowledge should not end as documents. They should end as skills.

This is especially true for SOPs, workflows, best practices, safety rules, audit standards, interaction templates, and operational checklists.

Once they become skills, their value changes from “I know this” into “I can reuse it, others can reuse it, agents can reuse it, and future me can reuse it too.”

8. What Could Come Next

Section titled “8. What Could Come Next”

Natural next steps include adding a stronger README, release notes, examples, and tighter integration with automated audit tasks. The same method can also be generalized into more guide skills for deployment, operations, security, channel configuration, and troubleshooting.

9. Closing Thought

Section titled “9. Closing Thought”

At its core, skill-vetter-guide is a practical optimization: it turns scattered, personal, easy-to-forget operational experience into a skill that is shareable, reusable, portable, and directly readable by agents.

Turning SOPs, workflows, and best practices into a skill is not just about sharing knowledge — it is about sharing a capability that can be used immediately.

That is far more practical than publishing a tutorial alone.

Why Does OpenClaw Still Require Approval for Long Commands Even with Default Allow?

Apr 3, 2026
Vibe Sparking

A source code investigation into OpenClaw’s exec approval mechanism

The Problem: Default Allow Set, but Long File Writes Still Need Approval

Section titled “The Problem: Default Allow Set, but Long File Writes Still Need Approval”

While using OpenClaw to auto-generate bilingual blog posts, I hit a counterintuitive issue.

The ~/.openclaw/exec-approvals.json default policy was already set to:

This should mean most exec commands run without approval prompts.

Yet in practice, the Chinese article wrote successfully, but the English version triggered an approval prompt:

If the default is already “allow,” why would a “command too long” error still require approval?

To find out, I dug into OpenClaw’s installation directory and latest source code.

The Trigger

Section titled “The Trigger”

The command in question was a heredoc writing an entire English article to a file:

The command itself isn’t dangerous — it’s just writing heredoc content to a file. But because the entire article was embedded in the command string, the total command length was very long. OpenClaw flagged it as:

  • Command too long
  • Potential obfuscation risk
  • Requires explicit approval

This wasn’t the regular exec permission policy — it was a higher-priority security interception.

The Investigation

Section titled “The Investigation”

Step 1: Verify Configuration

Section titled “Step 1: Verify Configuration”

Confirmed OpenClaw version (2026.4.2) and the approval config file. The defaults were indeed security: "full" + ask: "off" + askFallback: "full".

The regular exec allow configuration was correct.

Step 2: Locate the Error Source

Section titled “Step 2: Locate the Error Source”

Searched the OpenClaw installation directory for the error message, which led to the obfuscation detection module exec-obfuscation-detect.ts.

Key finding — a hardcoded constant:

And the detection logic:

Any command longer than 10,000 characters gets flagged as obfuscation detected.

Step 3: Check if Default Allow Can Override

Section titled “Step 3: Check if Default Allow Can Override”

Traced the gateway execution logic:

Once obfuscation is detected, the command enters the requiresAsk branch regardless of ask: "off".

Step 4: Search for a Skip Switch

Section titled “Step 4: Search for a Skip Switch”

Searched the source code for skipObfuscation, bypassObfuscation, disableObfuscation, and similar terms.

Result: No skip, disable, or exemption configuration exists.

  • MAX_COMMAND_CHARS = 10_000 is hardcoded
  • obfuscation.detected unconditionally forces approval
  • No public config can disable this rule

Step 5: Confirm Timeout Fallback Behavior

Section titled “Step 5: Confirm Timeout Fallback Behavior”

Normally, askFallback: "full" auto-approves on timeout. But obfuscation detection is an exception:

Obfuscated commands are denied even on approval timeout — no fallback.

Full Detection Rules

Section titled “Full Detection Rules”

Beyond command length, OpenClaw checks for these obfuscation patterns:

RuleDescription
command-too-longCommand exceeds 10,000 characters
base64-pipe-execBase64 decode piped to shell
hex-pipe-execxxd decode piped to shell
printf-pipe-execprintf escape sequences piped to shell
eval-decodeeval with encoded/decoded input
pipe-to-shellContent piped directly to shell interpreter
shell-heredoc-execShell heredoc execution
curl-pipe-shellRemote content piped to shell (has safe URL allowlist)
octal-escapeBash octal escape sequences
hex-escapeBash hex escape sequences
python-exec-encodedPython/Perl/Ruby encoded execution
var-expansion-obfuscationVariable assignment chain with expansion

These rules form OpenClaw’s command security layer, operating independently from the permission management layer.

Conclusion

Section titled “Conclusion”

Two-Layer Control

Section titled “Two-Layer Control”

OpenClaw implements two distinct control dimensions at the exec layer:

  1. Approval Policy Layer — Managed by exec-approvals.json: default allow, ask behavior, fallback
  2. Security Detection Layer — Intercepts suspicious command patterns, takes priority over the policy layer

Even with permissions wide open, the security layer can still block suspicious commands.

The Right Workaround

Section titled “The Right Workaround”

Since this rule can’t be disabled, the solution is to change how you write files:

Option 1: write + cp Use OpenClaw’s write tool to create the file in the workspace (bypasses shell entirely), then use a short cp command to move it to the target path.

Option 2: Split writes Don’t stuff an entire article into one heredoc. Split into multiple cat >> appends, each under 10KB.

Option 3: Core principle Let shell handle file transport, not file content.

One-Line Summary

Section titled “One-Line Summary”

OpenClaw’s default allow only affects regular exec approvals — it doesn’t bypass obfuscation detection. For long text file writes, use tool-based file creation + short shell commands for copying.

OpenClaw Exec Approval Bypass Guide: 4 Approvals to Turn Off Approvals

Apr 2, 2026
Vibe Sparking

OpenClaw Exec Approval Bypass Guide: 4 Approvals to Turn Off Approvals

Section titled “OpenClaw Exec Approval Bypass Guide: 4 Approvals to Turn Off Approvals”

Every cat triggers an approval popup? From principles to config in one guide, plus a real Bootstrap Paradox story.

The Problem: Every Command Needs a Click

Section titled “The Problem: Every Command Needs a Click”

After upgrading to OpenClaw v2026.4.1, you may notice — every shell command the agent runs triggers “Exec approval needed”, requiring manual approval.

Reading a file? Popup. Running grep? Popup. Cat a config? Popup.

It’s not a bug, it’s a feature. OpenClaw’s Exec Approval mechanism is a safety guardrail preventing AI agents from running dangerous commands without your knowledge. Good intention, but for self-managed local instances, the interaction cost is too high.

How It Works: Three Layers Decide a Command’s Fate

Section titled “How It Works: Three Layers Decide a Command’s Fate”

Configured in ~/.openclaw/exec-approvals.json:

1. Security Level

Section titled “1. Security Level”
ValueBehavior
denyBlock everything
allowlistOnly allowlisted commands pass
fullAllow everything

2. Ask (Popup Behavior)

Section titled “2. Ask (Popup Behavior)”
ValueBehavior
alwaysAsk for every command
on-missAsk only when not allowlisted
offNever ask

3. Ask Fallback (When No UI Available)

Section titled “3. Ask Fallback (When No UI Available)”
ValueBehavior
denyReject
allowlistAllow if allowlisted
fullAllow everything

Default is roughly security: "deny" + ask: "on-miss" — nearly every command triggers a popup.

Three Approaches

Section titled “Three Approaches”

Option 1: Progressive Allowlist (For the Cautious)

Section titled “Option 1: Progressive Allowlist (For the Cautious)”

Choose “Always allow” instead of “Allow once” each time. After a few days, common commands pass silently.

autoAllowSkills: true auto-allows CLI tools referenced by installed skills.

Good for: Shared instances, production, audit-required environments.

Option 2: Full Bypass (For Self-Managed)

Section titled “Option 2: Full Bypass (For Self-Managed)”

Three words: never ask again.

Good for: Local dev machines, personal instances, you-are-the-admin scenarios.

Option 3: Visual Configuration via Control UI

Section titled “Option 3: Visual Configuration via Control UI”

Web UI → Nodes → Exec approvals card. Click to configure, no JSON editing needed.

How To

Section titled “How To”

Config file: ~/.openclaw/exec-approvals.json

For Option 2, change the "defaults" field to:

Takes effect immediately — no gateway restart needed.

Rolling Back

Section titled “Rolling Back”

Your allowlist is preserved.

Per-Agent Fine Control

Section titled “Per-Agent Fine Control”

For multi-agent setups, only unlock specific agents:

defaults covers agents without individual config. agents.<id> overrides defaults.

Appendix: The Bootstrap Paradox

Section titled “Appendix: The Bootstrap Paradox”

Here’s the actual process of turning off Exec Approval — note the recursive irony:

Approval #1: Search for exec-approvals docs

Approval #2: Read the official documentation

Approval #3: View current config

Approval #4: Modify config to disable approvals

“Last approval ever 🎉 After this one, exec approval will never bother you again.”

4 approvals to complete “turn off approvals.” Classic Bootstrap Paradox — you need the key to get the key. At least you only need to forge it once.

Summary

Section titled “Summary”
Who You AreRecommendedKey Config
Local dev / PersonalFull bypasssecurity: full + ask: off
Shared / ProductionProgressive allowlistsecurity: allowlist + ask: on-miss + autoAllowSkills
Maximum securityManual allowlistsecurity: allowlist + ask: always

Exec Approval is good design, but good design must match the use case. For self-managing admins, popups aren’t security — they’re friction.

Based on OpenClaw v2026.4.1, config file ~/.openclaw/exec-approvals.json.
