OpenClaw Multi-Agent Permissions ≠ User Isolation: A Dangerous Misconception

Mar 29, 2026
Vibe Sparking

Think assigning different Agents to different users makes you secure? The Gateway trust model says otherwise.

What the Misconception Looks Like

Section titled “What the Misconception Looks Like”

When people first encounter OpenClaw’s multi-agent configuration, a natural thought emerges:

“I’ll create 3 Agents—admin for myself, developer for colleagues, viewer for external users—each with separate permissions. That’s user isolation, right?”

The config looks clean enough:

Three Agents, three permission sets, each with a clear role. Perfect?

No. This is a dangerous security illusion.

Why It Doesn’t Work: The Gateway Trust Model

Section titled “Why It Doesn’t Work: The Gateway Trust Model”

Core Fact: One Gateway = One Trust Domain

Section titled “Core Fact: One Gateway = One Trust Domain”

The official OpenClaw documentation is explicit:

Inside one Gateway instance, authenticated operator access is a trusted control-plane role, not a per-user tenant role.

In plain English:

  • Anyone who can connect to the Gateway is an operator
  • Operators have no hierarchy—there’s no “super admin” vs “regular user”
  • All operators have equal access to the Gateway’s control plane

What This Means in Practice

Section titled “What This Means in Practice”

Anyone with Gateway authentication (token or password), regardless of which Agent they’re “assigned” to, can:

ActionPossible?Consequence
List all Agents’ sessions✅ YesKnow who’s using what
Read other Agents’ chat history✅ YesSee all of admin’s conversations
Send messages to admin Agent’s session✅ YesExecute tools with admin’s permissions
Access Gateway API endpoints✅ YesFull control-plane operations

You configured deny: ["*"] for the viewer, but they can send messages directly to admin’s session and execute anything through admin’s permissions.

It’s like giving an intern a keycard that only opens the conference room—while the building’s back door is wide open.

A More Visual Explanation

Section titled “A More Visual Explanation”

sessionKey Is Not an Auth Token

Section titled “sessionKey Is Not an Auth Token”

Another common misunderstanding:

“Different Agents use different sessionKeys—surely the other party can’t get in without knowing the key?”

The official docs are clear:

Session identifiers (sessionKey, session IDs, labels) are routing selectors, not authorization tokens.

A sessionKey tells the Gateway “which conversation context I want to interact with”—it’s an address, not a lock. Knowing your street address doesn’t mean having your house key, but in the Gateway trust model, all operators hold the same master key.

What Multi-Agent Permissions Actually “Separate”

Section titled “What Multi-Agent Permissions Actually “Separate””

Let’s clarify the capability boundary:

✅ What It Can Do

Section titled “✅ What It Can Do”
  • Restrict the AI’s tool invocation scope — The viewer Agent’s AI truly can only call read, not exec
  • Reduce accidental AI misuse — Different Agents stay in their lanes
  • Functional partitioning within a trust domain — Your development Agent and messaging Agent stay separate

❌ What It Cannot Do

Section titled “❌ What It Cannot Do”
  • Prevent people from accessing other Agents’ data — The control plane is shared
  • Block privilege escalation via other Agents’ sessions — You can send messages to high-privilege Agents
  • Provide OS-level or filesystem-level isolation — Same machine, same user
  • Serve as a multi-tenant security boundary — It was never designed for this

One-line summary:

Multi-agent permissions constrain what the AI can do, not what people can see. To isolate people, isolate Gateways.

When Multi-Agent Permissions Are Appropriate

Section titled “When Multi-Agent Permissions Are Appropriate”
ScenarioSecure?Notes
One person, multiple purposes✅ Perfectly fineDev Agent and support Agent separated, reducing AI overreach
Same trust-domain team⚠️ AcceptableColleagues trust each other; prevents accidents, not malice
Family members sharing⚠️ Depends on trustFine if you don’t mind family seeing your chat history
Untrusted collaborators❌ Not secureEither party can access the full control plane
Public-facing service❌ Not secureExternal users = operators, catastrophic consequences
Client / vendor separation❌ Not secureVendor can see all client data

The Right Way to Isolate Users

Section titled “The Right Way to Isolate Users”

Option 1: One Gateway Per Person (Recommended)

Section titled “Option 1: One Gateway Per Person (Recommended)”
  • Each trust boundary gets its own Gateway instance
  • Separate OS users (ideally separate hosts / VPS)
  • Independent credentials, filesystems, configurations
  • Physical isolation = real isolation

Option 2: Same Machine, Different OS Users (Minimum)

Section titled “Option 2: Same Machine, Different OS Users (Minimum)”
  • Multiple OS users on the same machine
  • Each with their own ~/.openclaw directory
  • File permission isolation (ensure 0700)
  • Different ports, different auth tokens

Option 3: Container Isolation

Section titled “Option 3: Container Isolation”
  • One container per user
  • Network and filesystem naturally isolated
  • Ideal for team deployments

If You’re Already Using Multi-Agent “Isolation”…

Section titled “If You’re Already Using Multi-Agent “Isolation”…”

Check Immediately

Section titled “Check Immediately”

  1. Run a security audit:

    Watch for security.trust_model.multi_user_heuristic — the audit tool detects “config looks like multi-user but is actually single Gateway” situations.

  2. Verify Gateway auth token distribution — Who has the token? If untrusted parties have it, your “viewer” permissions are meaningless.

  3. Review channel configuration — Who can trigger the bot in Telegram / Slack? Everyone who can trigger it is an operator.

Migration Path

Section titled “Migration Path”

If you find your current setup is insecure:

  1. Create independent Gateway configurations for each trust boundary
  2. Migrate respective Agent configs and credentials
  3. Update channel bindings (each Gateway binds to its own bot)
  4. Revoke the old shared token
  5. Run openclaw security audit again

Suggestions for the OpenClaw Team

Section titled “Suggestions for the OpenClaw Team”

The current trust model is clear, documented, and intentional—a personal assistant doesn’t need multi-tenancy. But as use cases expand, the community needs:

  1. Prominent warnings in Agent configuration docs — Currently, agent permission config and security docs are separate; it’s easy to read only the former and assume “this is enough”
  2. Enhanced multi-user detection in openclaw security audit — When multiple agents + multiple channel sources are detected, proactively warn about trust model limitations
  3. Long-term consideration for per-user permission layers — Supporting user-level access control without splitting Gateways, reducing operational overhead for multi-person scenarios

One-Line Takeaway

Section titled “One-Line Takeaway”

Multi-agent permissions govern what the AI can do, not what people can see. To isolate people, isolate Gateways.

Don’t let a tidy config file give you a false sense of security.

Based on analysis of official OpenClaw security documentation (docs.openclaw.ai/gateway/security). Last updated: 2026-03-29

  • OpenClaw
  • Security
  • Multi-Agent
  • Trust Model
  • User Isolation

OpenClaw Permission Control Deep Dive: From 9-Layer Security to Production-Grade Hardening

Mar 29, 2026
Vibe Sparking

A comprehensive guide to OpenClaw’s tool permission system — combining official documentation and community best practices. Not just configuration templates, but a deep look at the trust model, audit mechanisms, and architecture trade-offs.

Why Permission Control Is OpenClaw’s Core Challenge

Section titled “Why Permission Control Is OpenClaw’s Core Challenge”

OpenClaw is not a chatbot — it’s an AI assistant platform with real system capabilities: file read/write, command execution, message sending, browser control, and more. A single prompt injection, if permissions aren’t locked down, could turn into an rm -rf or a bizarre email to your boss.

The fundamental question of permission control: How do you make AI powerful enough without letting it cross the line?

Part 1: Trust Model — The Foundation of All Configuration

Section titled “Part 1: Trust Model — The Foundation of All Configuration”

Personal Assistant Model, Not Multi-Tenant Platform

Section titled “Personal Assistant Model, Not Multi-Tenant Platform”

This is the most easily overlooked yet most important point:

OpenClaw’s security model is a personal assistant model — one Gateway instance = one trust boundary.

This means:

  • All users within a single Gateway share the same tool permissions. There’s no permission isolation between sessions; sessionKey is a routing selector, not an authentication token.
  • If multiple people share a bot (e.g., everyone in a Slack group can @it), every person can trigger all tool calls that agent is allowed to make.
  • Need real user isolation? Split your Gateways — use different Gateway instances for different trust boundaries, ideally running under different OS users or even different machines.

Real-World Consequences

Section titled “Real-World Consequences”
ScenarioRiskCorrect Approach
Company Slack group sharing one botAnyone can drive exec/file operations via promptsDedicated machine + dedicated OS user + minimal permissions
Personal multi-channel (Telegram + WhatsApp)Same trust domain, acceptableEnsure DM pairing + group requireMention
Family sharingFamily trust level determines configSensitive operations on separate Gateway

Part 2: The 9-Layer Permission Security Model

Section titled “Part 2: The 9-Layer Permission Security Model”

Every time AI calls a tool (read files, execute commands, send messages…), it must pass through 9 gates in sequence — blocked at any gate means termination. Layers go from coarse to fine:

Three Iron Rules

Section titled “Three Iron Rules”
  1. deny is irreversible — once any layer denies a tool, no subsequent layer can restore it
  2. Only tightening — later layers only get stricter, never re-enable what earlier layers disabled
  3. Fine overrides coarse — agent-level config overrides global; sender-level overrides group-level

⚠️ Common pitfall: Using deny: ["exec"] at Layer 1 to disable command execution, then allow: ["exec"] at Layer 5 for a specific agent — doesn’t work, exec is already dead. You can only fix it at Layer 1.

Part 3: Four Base Permission Tiers

Section titled “Part 3: Four Base Permission Tiers”

tools.profile is the starting point for permission configuration. OpenClaw provides 4 presets:

minimal — Minimum Permissions

Section titled “minimal — Minimum Permissions”
  • ✅ Status queries only, no file/command/message operations
  • Use case: Public services, demo environments, zero-trust scenarios

coding — Development Mode ⭐ Most Common

Section titled “coding — Development Mode ⭐ Most Common”
  • ✅ File read/write, command execution, session management, memory operations
  • Use case: Daily development, operations, project management

messaging — Messaging Mode

Section titled “messaging — Messaging Mode”
  • ✅ Chat session-related operations
  • ❌ No system files or commands
  • Use case: Customer service, message broadcasting, pure conversation bots

full — Full Access Mode

Section titled “full — Full Access Mode”
  • ⚠️ No restrictions whatsoever, admin use only
  • Official recommendation: Start with messaging or coding, open up as needed

Part 4: Fine-Grained Permission Configuration in Practice

Section titled “Part 4: Fine-Grained Permission Configuration in Practice”

4.1 Global Allow/Deny Lists

Section titled “4.1 Global Allow/Deny Lists”

Allow filesystem group tools but deny write operations = read-only filesystem

Tool Group Quick Reference:

  • group:fs — Filesystem (read/write/edit/apply_patch)
  • group:runtime — Runtime (exec/process)
  • group:automation — Automation (cron/gateway/browser)

4.2 Per-AI-Provider Differentiation

Section titled “4.2 Per-AI-Provider Differentiation”

Tighten permissions for cheaper/smaller models — smaller models are more susceptible to prompt injection, which is why the official audit checks models.small_params.

4.3 Multi-Agent Role Separation

Section titled “4.3 Multi-Agent Role Separation”

4.4 Sandbox Isolation

Section titled “4.4 Sandbox Isolation”

⚠️ Critical trap: Configuring sandbox.docker but not setting mode to "all" = sandbox is inactive. In this case, exec host=sandbox actually runs on the Gateway host! The official audit checks sandbox.docker_config_mode_off.

4.5 Sub-Agent Permissions

Section titled “4.5 Sub-Agent Permissions”

Sub-agents already have session operations disabled by default; this further locks down the control plane and automation tools.

4.6 Group / Channel / Sender-Level Control

Section titled “4.6 Group / Channel / Sender-Level Control”

All groups deny exec by default → specific group even stricter → but a specific user in that group gets exec back. This is the full capability of Layer 9.

Part 5: Security Auditing — Not Optional

Section titled “Part 5: Security Auditing — Not Optional”

Run Audits Regularly

Section titled “Run Audits Regularly”

Key Audit Items (Sorted by Severity)

Section titled “Key Audit Items (Sorted by Severity)”
SeverityCheckDescription
🔴 criticalgateway.bind_no_authRemote binding without authentication
🔴 criticalgateway.tailscale_funnelPublic internet exposure
🔴 criticalfs.state_dir.perms_world_writableState directory is world-writable
🔴 criticalsandbox.dangerous_network_modeDocker using host network mode
🔴 criticalsecurity.exposure.open_groups_with_elevatedOpen groups + elevated tools
🟡 warntools.exec.security_full_configuredexec bypasses approval
🟡 warntools.exec.auto_allow_skills_enabledSkills auto-trusted for exec
🟡 warnsandbox.docker_config_mode_offSandbox configured but not active
🟡 warntools.profile_minimal_overriddenAgent overrides global minimal

Credential Storage Locations

Section titled “Credential Storage Locations”

Paths to watch for auditing or backup:

Part 6: 5 Production-Grade Configuration Templates

Section titled “Part 6: 5 Production-Grade Configuration Templates”

Template 1: Read-Only Safe AI

Section titled “Template 1: Read-Only Safe AI”

Template 2: Safe Development AI (Read & Run, No Write)

Section titled “Template 2: Safe Development AI (Read & Run, No Write)”

Template 3: Pure Messaging AI

Section titled “Template 3: Pure Messaging AI”

Template 4: Public Service (Sandbox + Minimal)

Section titled “Template 4: Public Service (Sandbox + Minimal)”

Template 5: Hardened Baseline (Official Recommended Starting Point)

Section titled “Template 5: Hardened Baseline (Official Recommended Starting Point)”

This is the official 60-second hardening baseline — lock everything first, then open up as needed.

Part 7: Comparison with Similar Products

Section titled “Part 7: Comparison with Similar Products”
DimensionOpenClawNanoClawNanobotIronClawPicoClawZeroClaw
FocusFull-featured personal AI assistantLightweight embedded agentMinimal bot frameworkSecurity-hardened editionUltra-minimal single-task agentZero-config quick start
Permission layers9-layer fine-grained control2-3 simplified layersBasic allow/denyDefault-deny + allowlistAlmost nonePreset security templates
Multi-agent✅ Full role separation⚠️ Limited❌ Single agent✅ Supported❌⚠️ Basic
SandboxDocker sandboxNoneNoneMandatory sandboxNoneOptional
Security auditBuilt-in CLI audit toolNoneNoneBuilt-in + mandatoryNoneBasic checks
Channel integration7+ platforms1-2API onlySame as OpenClawCLI only1-2
Trust modelExplicit personal assistantImplicit single-userNo clear definitionZero-trust defaultN/ASingle-user
Config complexityHigh (price of flexibility)LowVery lowMedium-highVery lowVery low
Best forPower users needing fine controlResource-constrained devicesQuick prototypesSecurity-first scenariosMinimal needsQuick exploration

Selection Guide

Section titled “Selection Guide”
  • Need multi-channel + multi-agent + fine permissions → OpenClaw
  • Security compliance is a hard requirement → IronClaw (default-deny everything)
  • Embedded / resource-constrained → NanoClaw / PicoClaw
  • Quick idea validation → ZeroClaw / Nanobot
  • OpenClaw too complex but need core features → Start with ZeroClaw, migrate as needed

Part 8: Future Evolution

Section titled “Part 8: Future Evolution”

Near-Term

Section titled “Near-Term”

  1. Dynamic runtime approval expansion — Currently only exec has ask mode; future may extend to browser, gateway, cron, and more tools with runtime approval prompts.

  2. Continuous auditing — Evolving from manual openclaw security audit to background continuous monitoring + real-time alerts via webhooks.

  3. Hot permission policy updates — Permission config changes taking effect immediately without Gateway restart.

Mid-Term Trends

Section titled “Mid-Term Trends”

  1. Conditional policy engine — Evolving from static JSON allow/deny to a policy language supporting conditional expressions (time ranges, IP ranges, call frequency, etc.).

  2. Per-user permission boundaries — Implementing user-level permission isolation without splitting Gateways, reducing operational cost for multi-user scenarios.

  3. Cross-Gateway federation management — Unified policy distribution and compliance auditing for multi-instance cluster scenarios.

Long-Term Outlook

Section titled “Long-Term Outlook”

  1. RBAC / ABAC model — Evolving from tool-level allow/deny to role/attribute-based access control, integrating with enterprise IAM systems.

  2. Audit log compliance export — Supporting audit log formats required by compliance frameworks like SOC2 / ISO27001.

  3. AI behavior analysis — Detecting anomalous tool usage behavior based on historical call patterns (e.g., sudden surge in exec calls).

Conclusion

Section titled “Conclusion”

OpenClaw’s permission control system is the most comprehensive among similar products, with the 9-layer model covering everything from global scope to individual senders. Core takeaways:

  1. Understand the trust model first — Personal assistant ≠ multi-tenant; shared bot = shared permissions
  2. deny irreversibility is by design — Guarantees the security chain only tightens
  3. Start from the hardened baseline — Lock everything first, open up as needed, not the other way around
  4. Regular auditing is not optional — openclaw security audit --deep should be a routine ops habit
  5. Small model + big permissions = high risk — The weaker the model, the easier it is to inject; permissions must be tightened accordingly

Permission configuration may look complex, but it boils down to one sentence: From outside to inside, from coarse to fine, only tighten, never loosen.

Based on OpenClaw official security documentation (docs.openclaw.ai/gateway/security) and community practices. Last updated: 2026-03-29

Claude Code v2.1.86 Deep Analysis: Stability Polish × Security Fixes × Token Economics

Mar 28, 2026
Vibe Sparking

This release is centered on stability and experience polish, with 28 total changes: 1 new feature, 2 improvements, and 25 fixes. Below is a full breakdown.

I. New Features

Section titled “I. New Features”

1. X-Claude-Code-Session-Id HTTP Header

Section titled “1. X-Claude-Code-Session-Id HTTP Header”

Background: Enterprises using API proxies/gateways (such as LiteLLM, Helicone, and Portkey) for cost tracking and rate limiting need to know which requests belong to the same Claude Code session. Previously, this required parsing conversation metadata from the JSON body — a fragile approach with real privacy implications.

Use cases:

  • Enterprise IT teams using proxies to aggregate per-developer token usage by coding session
  • Security auditing: tracking anomalously high-frequency sessions
  • Example: X-Claude-Code-Session-Id: sess_abc123 → the proxy buckets and aggregates by header directly, without touching the request body

Caveats:

  • Session IDs can be correlated to user behavior; proxy logs should be sanitized accordingly
  • Self-hosted proxies must pass this header through — make sure your WAF isn’t stripping it

Competitive comparison:

ProductSession tracking approach
Claude CodeDedicated HTTP header (new)
CursorBuilt-in dashboard; no session-level header exposed
Continue.devNo native solution; requires custom injection
CopilotGitHub backend analytics; no proxy-level granularity

Trend: As AI coding agents move into the enterprise, observability will become table stakes. Expect dedicated AI agent APM toolchains to emerge — essentially Datadog for AI agents.

2. .jj / .sl Added to VCS Exclusion List

Section titled “2. .jj / .sl Added to VCS Exclusion List”

Background: Jujutsu (.jj/) and Sapling (.sl/) are next-generation version control systems. Previously, Claude Code’s Grep and file completion would descend into these directories, surfacing large volumes of metadata noise.

Use cases:

  • Teams using Jujutsu to manage monorepos will no longer see object files from .jj/store/ appearing in @ file completions
  • Code searches will no longer match internal state files under .sl/

Caveats: If you need to debug VCS metadata, you will need to specify the path manually.

Competitive comparison:

  • VS Code: Driven by .gitignore; requires manually adding .jj
  • Cursor: No explicit Jujutsu/Sapling exclusion support yet
  • JetBrains: Has a Jujutsu plugin, but index exclusion requires manual configuration

Trend: Jujutsu is growing rapidly (already in wide use inside Google). Expect native support across IDEs and AI coding tools by late 2026.

II. Core Bug Fixes

Section titled “II. Core Bug Fixes”

3. --resume Throwing “tool_use ids without tool_result blocks”

Section titled “3. --resume Throwing “tool_use ids without tool_result blocks””

Background: v2.1.85 changed the session serialization format, causing restored sessions to contain tool_use blocks without corresponding tool_result entries — failing API validation. This was a backward-compatibility break.

Scenario: A developer creates a long session in v2.1.84, upgrades, then attempts to continue with claude --resume → immediate crash.

Caveats:

  • Serialization compatibility issues are common in long-lived agent workflows
  • If you have custom session persistence logic, ensure tool_use/tool_result blocks are always paired

Competitive comparison: Cursor and Copilot Chat use short-lived sessions and largely avoid cross-version resume issues. Claude Code’s --resume is a genuine differentiator, but it comes with a maintenance burden.

Trend: Agent session resume will become a critical capability. Expect a standardized serialization format for agent conversations to emerge.

4. Write/Edit/Read Failing on Files Outside the Project Root

Section titled “4. Write/Edit/Read Failing on Files Outside the Project Root”

Background: When conditional skills or rules are configured, Claude Code’s file operation tools would error on paths outside the project root, such as ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md. The path validation logic in conditional skills was too strict, confining all paths to the project root.

Scenarios:

  • A user maintains global instructions in ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md
  • The agent attempts to read or edit that file → blocked by the conditional skill’s sandboxing logic

Caveats: This exposes a granularity problem in the security model — the tension between “enforcing project boundaries” and “allowing access to global configuration.”

Competitive comparison:

  • Cursor: Rules files are project-scoped only; this issue does not arise, but global rules are also not supported
  • Windsurf: Similar global + project-level configuration layering
  • Copilot: Instruction files are in a fixed location with no conditional loading logic

Trend: Permission models for AI coding agents will increasingly resemble OS-level file permissions — requiring allow-lists and layered policies.

5. Unnecessary Config Disk Writes on Every Skill Invocation

Section titled “5. Unnecessary Config Disk Writes on Every Skill Invocation”

Background: Every skill invocation was triggering a full config file write to disk. This was particularly bad on Windows, where NTFS performs poorly under frequent small writes, and concurrent writes could lead to config corruption.

Scenarios:

  • Windows users with heavy custom skill usage notice Claude Code getting progressively slower
  • In edge cases: config file gets corrupted by concurrent writes and requires manual repair

Caveats:

  • This is a classic write amplification problem
  • Windows users should verify config file integrity after upgrading

Competitive comparison: Most competing products use in-memory caching with debounced writes — this was a gap in Claude Code’s engineering maturity.

6. /feedback OOM Crash on Very Long Sessions

Section titled “6. /feedback OOM Crash on Very Long Sessions”

Background: The /feedback command serializes the entire session transcript before sending it. For marathon sessions spanning thousands of turns, the transcript can reach hundreds of megabytes — loading it all at once causes a Node.js heap out-of-memory crash.

Scenario: A developer working through an 8-hour coding session tries to submit feedback → the process is killed.

Caveats: This is also a reminder of good practice — start new sessions periodically rather than extending a single session indefinitely.

Competitive comparison:

  • Cursor: Each Composer interaction is independent; very long sessions are not an issue
  • Copilot Chat: Session length has an implicit cap

Trend: Agent “session lifecycle management” will become a product design priority. Analogous to browser tab management, agents will need session pruning, archival, and summarization.

7. --bare Mode Missing MCP Tools + Silently Dropping Messages

Section titled “7. --bare Mode Missing MCP Tools + Silently Dropping Messages”

Background: --bare mode (minimal UI, designed for embedding) had two independent bugs:

  1. MCP tools were not injected into the tool list
  2. Messages enqueued mid-turn were silently dropped

Scenarios:

  • Using --bare to embed Claude Code in a custom IDE/workflow → MCP tools (e.g., database queries) unavailable
  • Sending concurrent messages to a bare session → messages lost with no error

Caveats: --bare is an integration-facing interface; these bugs affect developers building on top of Claude Code.

Trend: Claude Code is evolving from a terminal tool into an embeddable agent runtime. The quality of --bare mode directly determines the ceiling of the ecosystem built around it.

III. Terminal UI Fixes

Section titled “III. Terminal UI Fixes”

Items 8-12: A Series of Targeted Terminal Experience Fixes

Section titled “Items 8-12: A Series of Targeted Terminal Experience Fixes”
BugRoot CauseImpact
c shortcut only copies ~20 characters of OAuth URLClipboard write length truncationOAuth login broken
OAuth password input leaks token prefix in narrow terminalsMasked input exposes plaintext on line wrapSecurity issue
Plugin scripts: Permission denied (macOS/Linux)Regression introduced in v2.1.83; files not marked +xAll marketplace plugins broken
Status line shows another instance’s model nameRace condition when multiple instances share stateUser misjudges current model
New messages not followed after scrollingScroll lock state not correctly resetRequires manual scroll to bottom

The OAuth token leak (item 9) deserves special attention — this is a real security vulnerability. In a narrow terminal (e.g., a split tmux pane), pasting an OAuth code causes the masked input’s line-wrapping logic to expose the first few characters of the token. While those characters alone are not sufficient for an attack, they represent a genuine risk in shoulder-surfing or screen-recording scenarios.

Items 13-16: Interaction Detail Fixes

Section titled “Items 13-16: Interaction Detail Fixes”
BugDescription
/plugin uninstall n key behaves counterintuitivelyPressing n should mean “don’t keep data” → instead it triggers the uninstall flow
Blank transcript after pressing EnterRace condition: UI not rendered before response arrives
Ultrathink hint persists after deleting keywordState cleanup incomplete
Markdown/highlight render cache memory leakLong sessions: cache holds full content strings without releasing them

The memory leak (item 16) explains why a long-running Claude Code session gets progressively sluggish — the markdown renderer’s cache grows without bound.

IV. Performance Improvements

Section titled “IV. Performance Improvements”

17. macOS Keychain Cache Extended from 5s to 30s

Section titled “17. macOS Keychain Cache Extended from 5s to 30s”

Background: Each claude.ai MCP connector queries the macOS Keychain for its token on startup. When multiple MCPs are configured, these Keychain calls execute serially, blocking the event loop and causing a noticeable startup delay.

Scenario: Five or more MCP connectors configured (GitHub, Jira, Slack, DB, custom) → startup takes several seconds.

Effect: Cache window extended from 5s to 30s; multiple connectors now share a single Keychain lookup.

Caveats: If you rotate a Keychain token within 30 seconds, you will need to restart Claude Code for the new token to take effect.

18. @ File References No Longer JSON-Escape Raw Content

Section titled “18. @ File References No Longer JSON-Escape Raw Content”

Background: When referencing a file with @filename, the content was being JSON string-escaped (\n → \\n, " → \"), adding unnecessary token overhead.

Scenario: Referencing a 1,000-line JSON file → escaped representation could consume 10-20% more tokens.

Effect: Raw strings are passed directly, reducing token usage and cost.

19. Read Tool: Compact Line Numbers + Deduplication of Unchanged Re-reads

Section titled “19. Read Tool: Compact Line Numbers + Deduplication of Unchanged Re-reads”

Background: The Read tool previously returned full file content on every call, even when the file had not changed. The line number format was also verbose.

Effect:

  • Compact line number format reduces token count
  • When the same file is read multiple times without changes, the content is deduplicated rather than consuming context window repeatedly

Combined impact of these three optimizations: For heavy users, a single session could see 5-15% token savings — translating directly to lower costs.

20. Improved Prompt Cache Hit Rates for Bedrock/Vertex/Foundry Users

Section titled “20. Improved Prompt Cache Hit Rates for Bedrock/Vertex/Foundry Users”

Background: Tool descriptions contained dynamic content (such as timestamps), causing the prompt prefix to differ on every request and resulting in cache misses.

Effect: Removing dynamic content makes tool descriptions static → stable prompt prefixes → consistent cache hits.

Competitive comparison: This leverages Anthropic API’s prompt caching feature. OpenAI’s prefix caching has similar optimization potential, but products like Cursor do not expose this level of control to users.

V. UX Improvements

Section titled “V. UX Improvements”

Items 21-25: Quality-of-Life Improvements

Section titled “Items 21-25: Quality-of-Life Improvements”
ImprovementDescription
Memory file names are now clickable/highlightedFile names in “Saved 3 memories” are now interactive links
/skills descriptions truncated at 250 charactersPrevents excessively long skill descriptions from consuming context
/skills sorted alphabeticallyFrom “arbitrary order” to “predictable order”
Auto mode shows reason when unavailableFrom a vague “currently unavailable” to “your plan does not support this”
[VSCode] Long operations no longer falsely report “Not responding”Timeout threshold raised or replaced with heartbeat detection
[VSCode] Max plan users downgraded to Sonnet after 8 hoursPlan information lost after OAuth token refresh

The VSCode Sonnet downgrade bug (item 25) is particularly painful — Max plan users paying for the highest tier are silently dropped to Sonnet after 8 hours, with a noticeable degradation in output quality and no notification whatsoever. This is a serious trust issue.

VI. Overall Assessment

Section titled “VI. Overall Assessment”

Release Positioning

Section titled “Release Positioning”

This is a classic stabilization release with minimal new features. The focus is squarely on:

  1. Reliability: Fixes for hard failures including resume crashes, OOM, and config corruption
  2. Security: OAuth token leak patched
  3. Performance: Token savings, faster startup, memory leak resolution
  4. Enterprise readiness: Session ID header, Bedrock/Vertex cache optimization

Overall Competitive Comparison

Section titled “Overall Competitive Comparison”
DimensionClaude CodeCursorCopilotWindsurf
Terminal-nativeCore strength---
Session resume--resume--Partial
Enterprise proxy supportNew headerDashboardGitHub backend-
Plugin ecosystemGrowingMatureMatureGrowing
StabilityRapid iterationRelatively stableStableRapid iteration
VCS breadthGit + Jujutsu + SaplingGit onlyGit onlyGit only

Future Trajectory

Section titled “Future Trajectory”
  1. Agent Runtime Evolution: The --bare mode fixes and Session ID header both point toward Claude Code evolving from a CLI tool into an embeddable agent runtime
  2. Enterprise-grade Observability: Session tracking → likely followed by span/trace support → a complete AI agent observability stack
  3. Session Lifecycle Management: The OOM fix is a stopgap; the long-term solution requires session pruning, auto-summarization, and segmented resume
  4. Multi-VCS World: Jujutsu support is a signal — development tooling in a post-Git era needs to be VCS-agnostic
  5. Token Economics: Three token optimizations shipped in a single release signals that Anthropic is serious about reducing API costs for users — a critical lever for retaining power users

Use Case: Users running Qwen series models (qwen-turbo, qwen-plus, qwen-max, etc.) as OpenClaw inference backends.

1.2 Doctor Auto-Migration Window Tightened

Section titled “1.2 Doctor Auto-Migration Window Tightened”

Background: openclaw doctor previously auto-fixed legacy config keys of any age. Now it only auto-migrates keys from within the last two months; older ones trigger an error instead.

Use Case: OpenClaw instances that haven’t been upgraded for a long time running openclaw doctor.

Example: If an instance hasn’t been upgraded for 3 months and its config contains old-format keys from late 2025, doctor will no longer silently fix them — it will report a validation error requiring manual intervention.

Notes:

  • ⚠️ Cluster instances may trigger this if they’ve been dormant for a while
  • Recommended: run openclaw doctor on the current version before upgrading to ensure config is up to date

Comparison: Most similar products are too new to have config migration issues. ZeroClaw has zeroclaw migrate openclaw but that’s a one-time import, not continuous migration.

Trend: A sound engineering decision — unlimited backward compatibility accumulates technical debt.

2. Providers & Models

Section titled “2.1 xAI / Grok: Responses API + x_search (#56048)”

Background: xAI (Elon Musk’s AI company) launched their Responses API (similar to OpenAI’s Responses API), along with x_search — a tool that can search X/Twitter real-time data. Previously, OpenClaw used xAI’s older Chat Completions API.

  • Search real-time trends, tweets, and public sentiment
  • Example: Ask “What are people discussing about AI Agents on X today?” → Grok uses x_search to pull real-time tweets

Notes:

  • The xAI plugin now auto-enables from web-search and tool config — no manual plugin activation needed
  • openclaw onboard and openclaw configure --section web now include x_search configuration options
  • x_search uses the shared xAI key — no additional API key required

Section titled “2.2 MiniMax Image Generation + Model Cleanup (#54487)”

Background: MiniMax is a Chinese AI company that launched the image-01 image generation model. Simultaneously, old models were cleaned up, retaining only M2.7.

Use Case:

  • Text-to-image: generate mode with aspect ratio control
  • Image-to-image: image-to-image editing mode

2.3 OpenAI apply_patch Enabled by Default

Section titled “2.3 OpenAI apply_patch Enabled by Default”

Background: apply_patch is OpenAI Codex’s code editing tool, previously requiring manual activation.

Use Case: Now available by default when using OpenAI or Codex models for code editing tasks.

Notes:

  • Sandbox policy aligned with write permissions — apply_patch permissions match file write permissions
  • Good news for ACP tasks using Codex in our cluster

Comparison: ZeroClaw and IronClaw haven’t implemented apply_patch yet. NanoClaw handles code editing inside containers due to its container isolation approach.

2.4 Mistral Request Standardization Fix

Section titled “2.4 Mistral Request Standardization Fix”

Background: Subtle differences between Mistral’s official API and OpenAI-compatible API request formats were causing 422 errors.

Use Case: Users connecting directly to Mistral’s official API (not via OpenRouter relay).

Notes: If you previously abandoned Mistral direct connection due to 422 errors, it’s worth trying again.

2.5 Google/Gemini Model Resolution Fix (#56567)

Section titled “2.5 Google/Gemini Model Resolution Fix (#56567)”

Background: Gemini 3.1’s pro/flash/flash-lite variants failed to resolve under different provider aliases, and flash-lite had prefix-matching order issues.

Use Case: Users configured with Google AI Studio, Vertex AI, or other Gemini provider aliases.

Notes: Fixed provider ID passthrough issues and added template-provider fallback. If Gemini flash-lite model switching wasn’t working before, it should be fine now.

2.6 Ollama thinking=off Fix (#53200)

Section titled “2.6 Ollama thinking=off Fix (#53200)”

Background: When thinkingLevel=off was set, Ollama models would still generate hidden reasoning tokens in the background, wasting compute and adding latency.

Use Case: Locally deployed Ollama running thinking-capable models (e.g., DeepSeek-R1, QwQ) where reasoning isn’t needed.

Notes: The fix now sends the think: false parameter. Important for resource-constrained devices — avoids unnecessary reasoning tokens.

Comparison: PicoClaw and ZeroClaw both support Ollama, but their thinking parameter control granularity doesn’t match OpenClaw’s.

2.7 Anthropic Stop Reason Handling (#56639)

Section titled “2.7 Anthropic Stop Reason Handling (#56639)”

Background: The Anthropic API sometimes returns non-standard stop reasons (e.g., sensitive — content safety block), which previously caused OpenClaw to crash.

Use Case: Any scenario using Claude models, especially when touching sensitive topics.

Notes: Now returned as a structured error instead of a crash. Important for cluster stability.

2.8 OpenAI Codex Image Tool Fix (#54829)

Section titled “2.8 OpenAI Codex Image Tool Fix (#54829)”

Background: Codex models were missing media-understanding provider registration, causing image analysis to fail.

Use Case: Using ACP to have Codex analyze screenshots, UI images, etc.

Notes: Also fixed generic image-runtime fallback (#54858), affecting third-party providers like OpenRouter and MiniMax Portal.

2.9 OpenAI WebSocket Reasoning Preservation (#53856)

Section titled “2.9 OpenAI WebSocket Reasoning Preservation (#53856)”

Background: In WebSocket mode, tool turns would lose reasoning replay metadata and tool-call item IDs, causing subsequent reasoning to break.

Use Case: Real-time interaction scenarios using OpenAI Responses API + WebSocket.

Notes: Two fixes (reasoning blocks restored + metadata kept intact) suggest this was a deep-seated issue.

2.10 GitHub Copilot Auth Refresh (#55360)

Section titled “2.10 GitHub Copilot Auth Refresh (#55360)”

Background: The expires_at value was treated as milliseconds when it was actually a seconds-level epoch, causing setTimeout to overflow and enter an infinite hot loop.

Use Case: Users running GitHub Copilot as a provider.

Notes: This was a performance bug — it would max out CPU. If you previously experienced system sluggishness after configuring Copilot, this was the cause.

2.11 Agent Model-Level Rate Limit Isolation (#49834)

Section titled “2.11 Agent Model-Level Rate Limit Isolation (#49834)”

Background: Previously, one model hitting 429 would block all models under the same auth profile.

Use Case: Configurations with multiple model fallbacks (e.g., Claude → GPT → Gemini).

Example: Claude hits 429, GPT should continue working, but previously the entire profile got cooled down.

Notes:

  • Cooldown strategy changed from exponential (1min → 1h) to stepped (30s / 1min / 5min) — more reasonable
  • New user-visible countdown messages
  • Important for heavily-used cluster instances

ZeroClaw✅ Trait-driven✅Basic

NanoClaw❌❌❌

2.12 Codex Failover Improvements (#55206, #42892)

Section titled “2.12 Codex Failover Improvements (#55206, #42892)”

Background: Codex’s accountId token extraction failures and server_error weren’t previously treated as failover-eligible errors.

Use Case: Automatic switching when Codex fails as an ACP backend.

Notes:

  • server_error now triggers failover
  • Codex error messages are cleaned before showing to users (no more raw error payloads and request_ids)
  • context-overflow guidance preserved for invalid_request_error

2.13 Agent Model Hot-Switching

Section titled “2.13 Agent Model Hot-Switching”

Background: Switching models mid-embedded-run previously waited for the current run to finish before taking effect.

Use Case: Using /model to switch to another model when the current one is overloaded or stuck.

Notes: Now switches at the next safe retry boundary without waiting for the entire run to complete. Noticeably improves responsiveness.

2.14 HTTP 410 as Retryable Error (#55201)

Section titled “2.14 HTTP 410 as Retryable Error (#55201)”

Background: Some providers return 410 Gone to indicate temporary unavailability, but it was previously treated as a permanent error.

Notes: 410 now defaults to timeout retry, while session-expired, billing, and auth signals are still correctly identified as non-retryable.

3.2 CLI Backend Plugin-ification

Section titled “3.2 CLI Backend Plugin-ification”

Background: The inference backends for Claude CLI, Codex CLI, and Gemini CLI were previously hardcoded — now moved to the plugin layer.

Use Case: Scenarios invoking Claude/Codex/Gemini through CLI tools (rather than API).

Notes:

  • gateway run --claude-cli-logs renamed to --cli-backend-logs (old flag still works)
  • Added Gemini CLI backend support
  • Config-referenced bundled plugins auto-load without manual plugins.allow

Trend: The “everything is a plugin” architectural direction — the core keeps getting thinner.

3.3 Plugin Auto-load

Section titled “3.3 Plugin Auto-load”

Background: Bundled provider and CLI-backend plugins previously required manual declaration in plugins.allow.

Use Case: New users configuring Claude CLI or Gemini CLI backends.

Notes: Lowers the configuration barrier, reducing “why did I configure it but it doesn’t work” issues.

3.4 Plugin Runtime Registration Isolation (#56101)

Section titled “3.4 Plugin Runtime Registration Isolation (#56101)”

Background: Plugin tools would register multiple times or load from the wrong runtime across multiple HTTP /tools/invoke calls.

Use Case: High-frequency plugin tool usage scenarios.

Notes: Fixes plugin tools “disappearing” or “registering twice.” Important for cluster stability.

3.5 Plugin SDK Path Resolution (#54283)

Section titled “3.5 Plugin SDK Path Resolution (#54283)”

Background: User plugins installed in ~/.openclaw/extensions/ couldn’t correctly resolve openclaw/plugin-sdk/* imports.

Use Case: Advanced users developing custom plugins.

3.6 Plugin Uninstall Cleanup (#35915)

Section titled “3.6 Plugin Uninstall Cleanup (#35915)”

Background: Uninstalling channel plugins didn’t clean up channels.<id> config, leaving residual entries.

Notes: Now shows an uninstall preview. Built-in channels and shared keys won’t be accidentally deleted.

3.7 Plugin Context Engines Compatibility (#50848)

Section titled “3.7 Plugin Context Engines Compatibility (#50848)”

Background: Newer versions of the assemble() call added a prompt field that older plugins didn’t recognize.

Notes: Auto-retry — tries new format first, falls back to old format on failure. Good backward compatibility strategy.

3.8 Bundled Diffs Plugin Fixes (#56077, #45869)

Section titled “3.8 Bundled Diffs Plugin Fixes (#56077, #45869)”

Background: Pierre diff viewer dependencies and theme loading would break after global install/update.

Use Case: Code diff viewing scenarios.

3.9 runHeartbeatOnce Exposed to Plugins (#40299)

Section titled “3.9 runHeartbeatOnce Exposed to Plugins (#40299)”

Background: Plugins couldn’t trigger a single heartbeat cycle.

Use Case:

  • A plugin wants to proactively trigger a heartbeat check after a specific event
  • Example: An email plugin triggers heartbeat upon receiving an important email, pushing info to the designated channel

Notes: Supports delivery target override, e.g., heartbeat: { target: "last" }.

4. ACP / Agent Runtime

Section titled “4. ACP / Agent Runtime”

4.1 ACP Current-Conversation Binds

Section titled “4.1 ACP Current-Conversation Binds”

Background: Previously, ACP spawn could only create child threads — it couldn’t directly bind to the current chat.

Use Case:

  • Launch a Codex workspace directly in the current Discord/iMessage/BlueBubbles conversation
  • Example: /acp spawn codex --bind here → the current chat becomes a Codex workspace without creating a child thread

Notes:

  • Documentation now clearly distinguishes three concepts: chat surface / ACP session / runtime workspace
  • Supported on Discord, BlueBubbles, and iMessage

Comparison: This is a feature unique to OpenClaw. Similar products don’t have the multi-channel ACP concept.

Trend: Agent integration with messaging platforms keeps deepening — from “call an agent within a chat” to “the chat itself is the agent workspace.”

4.2 ACPX Agent Registry Alignment (#28321)

Section titled “4.2 ACPX Agent Registry Alignment (#28321)”

Background: ACPX’s built-in agent mirror was inconsistent with the actual openclaw/acpx command defaults, and unknown agent IDs would be directly executed as commands.

Use Case: ACP harness routing to the wrong agent or executing unexpected commands.

Notes:

  • ⚠️ Security fix — Unknown agent IDs no longer fall through to raw command execution
  • npx built-ins pinned to exact version numbers

4.3 Agent Compaction Multiple Fixes (#49479, #51072, #46417, #45493)

Section titled “4.3 Agent Compaction Multiple Fixes (#49479, #51072, #46417, #45493)”

Background: Compaction (context compression) is a critical feature for long conversations. This release includes four related fixes:

  1. Post-compaction AGENTS refresh maintained in stale-usage preflight and queued followups
  2. Cancellation reason refinement — safeguard-specific cancel vs. manual /compact no-op distinction
  3. Timeout recovery — compress before high-context LLM timeout instead of retrying
  4. Count coordination — embedded auto-compaction success updates sessions.json

Use Case: Long-running agent sessions, especially during complex coding tasks.

Notes: #46417 is particularly important — previously, high-context timeouts would infinitely retry the same oversized request. Now it compresses first, then retries.

Comparison with Similar Products:

ProductContext CompactionAuto-TriggerTimeout Recovery

ZeroClaw✅ Basic✅❌

NanoClaw❌❌❌
PicoClawLimitedLimited❌

  2. 429/overload in embedded runs produced no user-visible reply
  3. Network errors (connection refused, DNS failure) were conflated with actual timeouts

Use Case: Any user encountering provider errors.

Notes: Error messages are now tiered: quota info is shown when available, HTML error pages get a generic fallback, and network errors vs. timeouts have distinct diagnostic messages.

  • Numerous channel-specific fixes (Telegram splitting, Discord reconnection, WhatsApp loops, Matrix encryption, etc.)

  • Heartbeat timer recovery

Comparison: This is a unique advantage of OpenClaw as the largest-install-base project (186K+ stars, 100K+ installations) — a massive user base means more edge cases discovered and fixed. Similar products haven’t reached this scale yet.

OpenClaw v2026.3.24 Stable: Teams SDK Migration, Sandbox Security Fix, 27 Bug Fixes

Mar 26, 2026
Vibe Sparking

OpenClaw v2026.3.24 Stable

Section titled “OpenClaw v2026.3.24 Stable”

Five days, four releases. v2026.3.22 broke records. v2026.3.23 patched 29 bugs in 48 hours. v2026.3.24-beta.1 landed 18 feature changes and 40+ fixes. Beta.2 ran a quick RC validation. Now the stable release is out, moving everything from beta.1 into the stable channel with 27 bug fixes.

This post won’t rehash beta.1 content. It focuses on fixes new to the stable release, the security change you need to know about, and how the beta-to-stable pipeline worked.

Reference: GitHub Release v2026.3.24

Beta to Stable: A 3-Day Convergence

Section titled “Beta to Stable: A 3-Day Convergence”

Beta.2 cherry-picked only 3 fixes for validation and shipped stable 2.5 hours later. The team was confident in beta.1’s quality. Beta.2 was a smoke test, not a regression sweep.

Feature Changes: Same as Beta.1

Section titled “Feature Changes: Same as Beta.1”

All 18 feature changes are identical to beta.1. Nothing added, nothing removed. If you read the beta.1 post, skip this section.

Key changes at a glance:

  • Gateway: /v1/models and /v1/embeddings endpoints, model parameter passthrough
  • Teams: Official SDK migration with streaming replies, welcome cards, AI labeling
  • Teams: Message edit and delete
  • Skills: Install metadata for 7 built-in skills with guided dependency setup
  • Control UI: Skills management overhaul with status filters and detail dialogs
  • Slack: Rich interactive reply consistency restored, Options: auto-renders as buttons
  • CLI: --container flag for Docker/Podman in-container execution
  • Discord: LLM-generated thread titles
  • Plugins: before_dispatch hook
  • Control UI/macOS: 6 UI improvements (file preview, tree navigation, model selector)
  • Runtime: Node 22 minimum lowered to 22.14
  • CLI: Node version preflight check before upgrade

Security Fix: Media Path Alias Sandbox Bypass

Section titled “Security Fix: Media Path Alias Sandbox Bypass”

This is the most important fix in this release.

Problem: Outbound tools and message actions could bypass media-root restrictions through mediaUrl or fileUrl alias fields, accessing files outside the sandbox. A malicious prompt injection could trick an agent into reading /etc/passwd via fileUrl and sending it externally.

Root cause: Security boundary checks only covered primary path fields. Alias fields were unchecked.

Impact: Multi-tenant OpenClaw deployments are at highest risk. Single-user setups are less exposed but should still upgrade.

Path traversal via alias fields is a classic web security issue. Jupyter Notebook and Code Server have both had similar vulnerabilities. This fix unifies all path fields under the same security check.

Bug Fixes: 16 Items in Stable Changelog

Section titled “Bug Fixes: 16 Items in Stable Changelog”

Outbound Media/Local Files: Policy Alignment

Section titled “Outbound Media/Local Files: Policy Alignment”

Sending host-machine local files failed when workspaceOnly was off. File sending used different permission logic than file reading. If you worked around this by copying files into the workspace, you can remove that workaround.

Gateway Restart Session Recovery

Section titled “Gateway Restart Session Recovery”

After a gateway restart, interrupted sessions got a best-effort restart notification but thread/topic routing information could be lost. Now uses heartbeat-based wakeup, preserves routing info, and retries failed outbound delivery once.

Docker First-Install Boot Loop

Section titled “Docker First-Install Boot Loop”

Fresh Docker installs got stuck in a loop: the CLI tried to connect to the gateway before it started, but the gateway needed config that the CLI was supposed to write. Classic chicken-and-egg. Fixed by writing config through the gateway process directly, bypassing network dependency.

Channel Startup Fault Isolation

Section titled “Channel Startup Fault Isolation”

An expired Telegram bot token would take down not just Telegram but Discord and WhatsApp too. Channels started serially with no try-catch isolation. Now each channel fails independently. This is the bulkhead pattern applied to channel startup.

WhatsApp Echo Suppression

Section titled “WhatsApp Echo Suppression”

In groups, gateway-sent messages were processed as new inbound messages, creating reply loops. The fix also stopped suppressing owner commands sent from linked accounts. Now tracks recently sent message IDs and only suppresses matching echoes.

WhatsApp Reply-to-Bot Detection

Section titled “WhatsApp Reply-to-Bot Detection”

Replying to a bot message in a group to trigger the bot stopped working. The bot’s selfLid was being read differently. WhatsApp’s linked account mode, where bot and owner share one number, is the root complexity here.

Telegram Forum #General Topic Routing

Section titled “Telegram Forum #General Topic Routing”

The #General topic (topic ID = 1) in Telegram forum mode failed to route when Telegram omitted forum metadata. If you use OpenClaw in Telegram forum groups, upgrade for this fix.

Discord Gateway Crash Elimination

Section titled “Discord Gateway Crash Elimination”

Discord server disconnects caused full process crashes instead of graceful reconnection. Lifecycle errors during startup, runtime, and teardown phases are now properly classified and handled.

Discord Timeout Visible Replies

Section titled “Discord Timeout Visible Replies”

When a Discord worker timed out (agent thinking too long), users saw nothing. Now sends a visible timeout message.

ACP Direct Chats TTS Empty Audio

Section titled “ACP Direct Chats TTS Empty Audio”

In voice conversation mode, if TTS synthesis failed, neither audio nor text was delivered. Now falls back to text delivery when TTS returns empty audio.

Telegram 403 Error Handling

Section titled “Telegram 403 Error Handling”

After a bot was kicked from a group, queued messages kept retrying forever. Now preserves specific 403 reasons (blocked/kicked/not a member) and marks “bot not a member” as permanent failure to stop retries.

Telegram Photo Size Preflight

Section titled “Telegram Photo Size Preflight”

Uploading photos that didn’t meet Telegram’s dimension requirements failed with PHOTO_INVALID_DIMENSIONS. Now checks dimensions before sending and falls back to document upload. Telegram rules: longest side under 1280px, aspect ratio under 20:1.

Slack DM Reply Optimization

Section titled “Slack DM Reply Optimization”

DM replies had unnecessary overhead, and web-search was triggered automatically when it shouldn’t have been. Streamlined reply logic, web-search changed to explicit opt-in.

Embedded Runs SecretRef Crash

Section titled “Embedded Runs SecretRef Crash”

Unresolved SecretRef configuration crashed embedded agent runs. Now falls back to the resolved runtime snapshot.

Hidden Fixes: In Beta.1 but Not Listed in Stable Changelog

Section titled “Hidden Fixes: In Beta.1 but Not Listed in Stable Changelog”

These shipped in beta.1, were validated through beta.2, and entered stable — but the stable changelog doesn’t list them individually.

  • Feishu SecretRef startup crash: Unresolved SecretRef treated as “not configured” instead of crashing
  • Feishu open group policy @mention filtering: Non-text messages in groupPolicy: open groups were blocked by implicit mention checks. After upgrade, bot receives all non-text messages in groups
  • Feishu @mention detection degradation: Bot identity fetch timeout raised to 30s with background recovery
  • Feishu/Teams card payload: Native card payload changed from required to optional
  • Feishu docx block ordering: Document block order scrambled when writing new documents
  • Google image model migration: openclaw doctor --fix didn’t set /v1beta path correctly
  • Custom Google provider paths: Custom-named providers lost /v1beta prefix
  • Telegram slash commands under SecretRef
  • Docker Compose port parsing: "8080:3000" format parsed incorrectly
  • LanceDB proxy environment embedding requests
  • Build stability: Hash chunk files or shell shims broken after local rebuilds
  • Skill installer security hardening: Regex whitelist, output sanitize, URL protocol restrictions, source warnings

Skill Installer Security Hardening Details

Section titled “Skill Installer Security Hardening Details”

Worth calling out separately:

  1. Install commands validated against a regex whitelist — only predefined package manager commands allowed
  2. Skill metadata sanitized before terminal output to prevent escape sequence injection
  3. URL fields restricted to http/https, blocking file:// and other protocols
  4. Non-built-in skill installs show source warnings
  5. Removed file:// workspace links

These hardening measures alongside the new /v1/models and other endpoints show the team taking security boundaries seriously while expanding functionality.

Upgrade Recommendations

Section titled “Upgrade Recommendations”

Must upgrade:

  • Multi-tenant OpenClaw (media path alias sandbox bypass)
  • Telegram forum groups (General topic routing fix)
  • Docker deployments that hit the first-install boot loop
  • WhatsApp groups with echo loops

Should upgrade:

  • Teams integration users (SDK migration is a full rewrite)
  • Gateway OpenAI compatibility needed
  • Slack rich interactive components

Can wait:

  • Single-channel, single-user deployments running stable

Upgrade:

If your Node.js version is below 22.14, the new version tells you before installing instead of crashing after.

Trends

Section titled “Trends”

Five days, four releases from v2026.3.22 to v2026.3.24. This pace reflects where OpenClaw is: alternating between feature expansion and stability convergence.

Directions to watch:

  • OpenAI compatibility layer is filling out. Assistants API and Realtime WebSocket proxy are likely next.
  • Plugin lifecycle hooks currently only have before_dispatch. A full message lifecycle hook system is coming.
  • Skill ecosystem moved from install metadata to security hardening, building toward a ClawHub marketplace.
  • Feishu got 5 bug fixes in one release, signaling growing adoption in China and active community feedback.

OpenClaw’s positioning in 2026 has shifted from “multi-channel bot” to “AI Agent platform.” Local-first, omnichannel delivery, programmable — that intersection has no direct competitor.

OpenClaw v2026.3.24-beta.1: Gateway Compat, Teams Rewrite, One-Click Skills, Container CLI

Mar 25, 2026
Vibe Sparking

OpenClaw v2026.3.24-beta.1

Section titled “OpenClaw v2026.3.24-beta.1”

Three releases in four days. v2026.3.22 was the biggest release in OpenClaw history. v2026.3.23 cleaned up 29 bugs within 48 hours. Now v2026.3.24-beta.1 lands with gateway compatibility changes, a full Microsoft Teams SDK migration, one-click skill installs, container CLI support, a Control UI overhaul, and another 40+ fixes.

The beta tag is honest: this moves fast, test before you deploy.

Reference: GitHub Release v2026.3.24-beta.1

Gateway: OpenAI Compatibility for RAG and Custom Clients

Section titled “Gateway: OpenAI Compatibility for RAG and Custom Clients”

The gateway now speaks more of the OpenAI API surface. Three changes, all from @vincentkoc.

/v1/models and /v1/embeddings. Tools like LangChain, LlamaIndex, and custom RAG pipelines that probe /v1/models before sending requests used to get 404s from OpenClaw’s gateway. Now they get a model list. Embedding endpoints work too.

Explicit model overrides. If a client sends a specific model name through /v1/chat/completions or /v1/responses, the gateway now forwards it instead of silently replacing it with the agent’s default. RAG orchestrators that route different queries to different models can now pass through OpenClaw without losing that routing.

If you’re using OpenClaw as a gateway in front of a RAG stack, this is the change that makes it work without wrapper hacks.

Microsoft Teams: Full SDK Migration

Section titled “Microsoft Teams: Full SDK Migration”

This isn’t a patch. The entire Teams integration has been rewritten on the official Microsoft Teams SDK. Two PRs — #51808 and #49925 — cover the full scope.

Streaming 1:1 replies. DM responses now stream token-by-token instead of arriving as a single block after the model finishes.

Welcome cards with prompt starters. New conversations show a card with suggested prompts so users don’t stare at an empty chat wondering what to type.

Feedback and reflection. Users can rate responses. The bot can reflect on its own output.

Typing indicators and status updates. The bot shows “typing…” while processing and sends informative status updates for long-running operations.

Native AI labeling. Messages from the bot are labeled as AI-generated, following Microsoft’s AI-agent UX guidelines.

Message edit and delete. Sent messages can be edited or deleted, including in-thread fallbacks when no explicit target is provided.

If your organization runs Teams and has been waiting for OpenClaw’s Teams support to feel production-ready, this is it.

Skills: One-Click Install and Status Filters

Section titled “Skills: One-Click Install and Status Filters”

Skills used to require reading docs, checking dependencies, and manually configuring API keys. Two changes make this simpler.

Install recipes on bundled skills. Seven bundled skills — coding-agent, gh-issues, openai-whisper-api, session-logs, tmux, trello, weather — now include install metadata. The CLI and Control UI can detect missing requirements and offer to install them. Thanks @BunsDev. (#53411)

Control UI status-filter tabs. The skills page now shows tabs: All / Ready / Needs Setup / Disabled, each with counts. Clicking a skill opens a detail dialog with requirements, a toggle switch, install action, API key entry, source metadata, and homepage link. The old inline cards are gone. Thanks @BunsDev. (#53411)

CLI improvements. The missing-requirements label softened from “missing” to “needs setup.” openclaw skills info now surfaces where to get an API key, the CLI save command, and the storage path. The macOS app shows a “Get your key” link and storage-path hint in the API key editor. Thanks @BunsDev. (#53411)

CLI: Run Commands Inside Containers

Section titled “CLI: Run Commands Inside Containers”

New --container flag and OPENCLAW_CONTAINER env var. Point any openclaw command at a running Docker or Podman OpenClaw container and it executes inside that container. Thanks @sallyom. (#52651)

Before:

After:

Works with any openclaw subcommand. No more shell-into-container-then-run workflows.

Control UI: Visual Overhaul

Section titled “Control UI: Visual Overhaul”

Five changes from @BunsDev that collectively redesign the Control UI. (#53411)

Agent workspace files. File rows in the agent workspace are now expandable <details> elements with lazy-loaded inline markdown preview. Comprehensive .sidebar-markdown styles cover headings, lists, code blocks, tables, blockquotes, and details/summary.

Markdown preview dialog. Frosted backdrop, properly sized panel, styled header, and @create-markdown/preview v2 system theme. Headings, tables, code blocks, callouts, and blockquotes auto-adapt to light/dark mode.

macOS app navigation. The horizontal pill-based subsection navigation is replaced with a collapsible tree sidebar using disclosure chevrons and indented rows.

Agent model selector. The default agent model dropdown now shows a “Not set” placeholder instead of being blank.

Live tools view. The /tools endpoint now shows what tools the current agent can actually use right now, with a compact default view and optional detailed mode. The Control UI adds a live “Available Right Now” section.

Slack: Rich Reply Parity Restored

Section titled “Slack: Rich Reply Parity Restored”

Rich reply formatting was broken for direct deliveries. Trailing Options: lines in responses now auto-render as buttons/selects. Interactive setup defaults improved. Reply controls are isolated from plugin interactive handlers. Thanks @vincentkoc. (#53389)

Discord: Auto-Thread Naming

Section titled “Discord: Auto-Thread Naming”

New optional autoThreadName: "generated" config. Auto-created threads can be renamed asynchronously with LLM-generated titles. The existing message-based naming remains the default. Thanks @davidguttman. (#43366)

Plugins: before_dispatch Hook

Section titled “Plugins: before_dispatch Hook”

New before_dispatch hook with canonical inbound metadata. Handled replies route through the normal final-delivery path, preserving TTS and routed delivery semantics. Thanks @gfzhx. (#50444)

Security Fixes

Section titled “Security Fixes”

Sandbox media bypass closed. The mediaUrl/fileUrl alias was a way to escape media-root restrictions on outbound tool and message actions. Closed. (#54034)

Skill installer validation. Skill installer metadata is now validated against strict regex allowlists per package manager. Skill metadata is sanitized for terminal output. URL protocol allowlisting applies to markdown preview and skill homepage links. Non-bundled skill install sources get a warning. Unsafe file:// workspace links are removed. Thanks @BunsDev. (#53471)

Bug Fixes: The Full List

Section titled “Bug Fixes: The Full List”

Gateway and Runtime

Section titled “Gateway and Runtime”

Restart sentinel. After a restart, the interrupted agent session now wakes via heartbeat instead of a best-effort restart note. Outbound delivery retries once on transient failure. Explicit thread/topic routing is preserved through the wake path. Thanks @VACInc. (#53940)

Docker setup loop. Fresh Docker installs were failing because the pre-start openclaw-cli onboard/config writes tried to reach a gateway that wasn’t up yet — creating a namespace loop. Setup-time writes now route through openclaw-gateway. Thanks @amsminn. (#53385)

Channel boot isolation. Channel startup stays sequential, but per-channel boot failures are now isolated. One broken channel no longer blocks the rest. Thanks @JonathanJing. (#54215)

Embedded run secrets. Unresolved SecretRef config no longer crashes embedded agent runs — falls back to the resolved runtime snapshot. Fixes #45838.

Gateway ports. Docker Compose-style OPENCLAW_GATEWAY_PORT host publish values parse correctly without reviving the legacy CLAWDBOT_GATEWAY_PORT override. Thanks @bebule. (#44083)

Runtime build. Lazy dist runtime entry paths and bundled plugin npm staging stabilized so local rebuilds stop breaking. Thanks @vincentkoc. (#53855)

WhatsApp

Section titled “WhatsApp”

Group echo suppression. The bot now tracks recent gateway-sent message IDs and suppresses only matching group echoes. Owner /status, /new, and /activation commands from linked-account fromMe traffic are preserved. Thanks @w-sss. (#53624)

Reply-to-bot detection. Implicit group reply detection restored by unwrapping botInvokeMessage payloads and reading selfLid from creds.json. Reply-based mentions reach the bot again in linked-account group chats.

Telegram

Section titled “Telegram”

Forum topic recovery. #General topic 1 routing recovered when Telegram omits forum metadata. Covers native commands, interactive callbacks, inbound message context, and fallback error replies. Thanks @huntharo. (#53699)

Outbound error handling. Actionable 403 membership/block/kick details preserved. Bot-not-a-member treated as permanent delivery failure — Telegram sends stop retrying doomed chats. Thanks @w-sss. (#53635)

Photo validation. Telegram photo dimension and aspect-ratio rules are checked before sending. Invalid or unavailable image metadata falls back to document sends instead of failing with PHOTO_INVALID_DIMENSIONS. Thanks @hnshah. (#52545)

Pairing codes. Rendered as Telegram-only code blocks while keeping shared pairing replies plain text for other channels. Thanks @sumukhj1219. (#52784)

Native commands. Slash-command execution runs against the resolved runtime snapshot so DM commands reply even when fresh config reads surface unresolved SecretRefs. Thanks @nimbleenigma. (#53179)

Topic creation from CLI. Message thread create routes through Telegram topic-create with the required topic name field. Thanks @andyliu. (#54336)

Discord

Section titled “Discord”

Gateway supervision. Gateway error handling centralized behind a lifetime-owned supervisor. Early, active, and late-teardown Carbon gateway errors stay classified consistently and stop surfacing as process-killing teardown crashes.

Timeout replies. A visible timeout reply is sent when the inbound worker times out before a final reply starts. Includes auto-thread targets and queued-run ordering. Thanks @Kimbo7870. (#53823)

Config types. Missing autoArchiveDuration added to DiscordGuildChannelConfig so TypeScript definitions match schema and runtime. Thanks @davidguttman. (#43427)

Feishu

Section titled “Feishu”

Startup crashes. Unresolved SecretRef app credentials treated as not-configured during account resolution. CLI startup and read-only Feishu config surfaces stop crashing. Thanks @hpt. (#53675)

Group policy. When groupPolicy is open, image, file, audio, and non-text group messages reach the bot without requiring @mentions, unless operators explicitly enable mention gating. Thanks @byungsker. (#54058)

Mention enforcement. requireMention enforcement stays strict when bot identity probes fail. Startup timeout raised to 30s. Cancellable background identity recovery added. Thanks @lefarcen. (#43788)

Card payloads. Provider-native card payloads made optional in merged tool schemas. Media-only sends stop failing validation. Thanks @lndyzwdxhs. (#53715)

Docx block ordering. Document tree order from docx.document.convert is preserved when inserting blocks. Heading/paragraph/list misordering in Feishu documents fixed. Thanks @TaoXieSZ. (#40524)

Slack

Section titled “Slack”

Runtime defaults. Slack DM reply overhead trimmed. Codex auto transport restored. DM preview threading, cache scoping, warning dedupe, and explicit web-search opt-in tightened. Thanks @vincentkoc. (#53957)

ACP

Section titled “ACP”

Direct chat delivery. A terminal ACP result is always delivered when final TTS doesn’t yield audio, even if block text already streamed. Redundant empty-text final synthesis skipped. Thanks @w-sss. (#53692)

Models and Providers

Section titled “Models and Providers”

Doctor/image generation. Migrated legacy Nano Banana Google provider config seeded with the /v1beta API root and an empty model list so openclaw doctor --fix completes. Thanks @mahopan. (#53757)

Google model normalization. Bare Google Generative AI API roots normalized for custom provider names. Built-in Google model-id rewrites work when api is declared only on individual models. Thanks @Kathie-yu. (#44969)

DeepSeek pricing. Zero-cost DeepSeek catalog rates replaced with current DeepSeek V3.2 pricing. Usage totals stop showing $0.00. Thanks @arkyu2077. (#54143)

Memory and Plugins

Section titled “Memory and Plugins”

LanceDB proxy. The env-configured HTTP/HTTPS proxy dispatcher bootstraps before OpenAI embeddings requests. Memory capture and recall work in proxy-required environments again. Thanks @neeravmakwana. (#54119)

Builtin SQLite memory. Redundant sync and status query churn reduced by snapshotting file state once per source, reusing sync statements, and consolidating status reads. Thanks @vincentkoc.

Plugin hooks. Terminal hook decision semantics enforced for tool/message guards. Thanks @joshavant. (#54241)

Agents and Cron

Section titled “Agents and Cron”

Cron heartbeat suppression. The default heartbeat system prompt is suppressed for cron-triggered embedded runs, even when targeting non-cron session keys. Cron tasks stop reading HEARTBEAT.md and polluting unrelated threads. Thanks @Protocol-zero-0. (#53152)

Cron delivery. Best-effort announce runs marked as not-delivered when any payload fails. Partial delivery failures logged instead of silently reporting success. Thanks @MoerAI. (#42535)

CLI and Tooling

Section titled “CLI and Tooling”

Log timestamps. Pretty log timestamps always include an explicit timezone offset in both default UTC and --local-time modes. Thanks @sahilsatralkar. (#38904)

Browser detection. macOS LaunchServices Edge bundle IDs recognized so Chromium detection stops falling back to Chrome when Edge is the system default. Thanks @zoherghadyali. (#48561)

Marketplace

Section titled “Marketplace”

ClawHub skill URL. Corrected the ClawHub skill URL in agent docs. Marketplace archive downloads stream to disk so installs avoid excess memory use. Thanks @QuinnH496. (#54160)

TUI

Section titled “TUI”

Chat history. Pending user messages preserved when a slow local run emits an empty final event. History reload deferred and flushed after the newer active run finishes. Silent/tool-only runs no longer stay incomplete. Thanks @joelnishanth. (#53130)

Docs

Section titled “Docs”

IRC examples. Five json55 code-fence typos fixed so Mintlify applies JSON5 syntax highlighting correctly. Thanks @Hollychou924. (#50842)

Upgrade

Section titled “Upgrade”

This is a pre-release beta. Test in staging before production.

If you’re still on v2026.3.22, go through v2026.3.23 first — the v2026.3.23 fixes are included here, but the migration path is smoother in sequence.

Contributors

Section titled “Contributors”

25+ contributors in this release: @vincentkoc, @BunsDev, @sallyom, @davidguttman, @gfzhx, @VACInc, @amsminn, @JonathanJing, @w-sss, @huntharo, @hnshah, @sumukhj1219, @nimbleenigma, @bebule, @neeravmakwana, @joshavant, @Protocol-zero-0, @MoerAI, @sahilsatralkar, @zoherghadyali, @QuinnH496, @joelnishanth, @Hollychou924, @hpt, @byungsker, @lefarcen, @lndyzwdxhs, @TaoXieSZ, @Kimbo7870, @mahopan, @Kathie-yu, @arkyu2077, @andyliu, @07akioni.
