OpenClaw v2026.3.23: 29 Fixes in 48 Hours — The Community Cleanup After the Big One

Mar 24, 2026
Vibe Sparking

OpenClaw v2026.3.23: 29 Fixes in 48 Hours

Section titled “OpenClaw v2026.3.23: 29 Fixes in 48 Hours”

You ship the biggest release in your project’s history. Ten breaking changes. Eighty-plus contributors. Then you wait.

The bug reports started within hours of v2026.3.22 landing. Browser tabs hanging on attach. ClawHub credentials invisible on macOS. Mistral models blowing past token limits. Gateway processes crash-looping under systemd. The community didn’t just report — they diagnosed, reproduced, and in many cases pointed straight at the root cause.

v2026.3.23 is the result: 29 targeted fixes, shipped 48 hours later. No new features. No breaking changes. Just repairs.

Reference: GitHub Issue #52808

Browser: Attach and Reuse Actually Work Now

Section titled “Browser: Attach and Reuse Actually Work Now”

Two fixes, both from @vincentkoc, both addressing the same root problem: the browser integration was too eager to declare success.

Chrome MCP attach timing. When you pointed OpenClaw at an already-running browser via Chrome MCP, the handshake completed before the tabs were actually usable. OpenClaw now waits for existing-session tabs to become interactive after attach instead of treating the initial protocol handshake as ready. (#52930)

CDP loopback reuse. If a loopback browser was already running but briefly unreachable — common during high CPU load or after wake from sleep — OpenClaw would skip it and fall back to relaunch detection. Now it retries the already-running instance through a short reachability window before giving up. (#53004)

Both fixes are invisible when things work. When they don’t, you get phantom browser launches and orphaned Chrome processes. That’s over.

ClawHub on macOS: Three Auth Paths, All Broken

Section titled “ClawHub on macOS: Three Auth Paths, All Broken”

v2026.3.22 made ClawHub the default plugin source. That means ClawHub auth is no longer optional — it’s load-bearing. On macOS, three separate auth resolution paths were silently failing.

macOS auth config. Saved ClawHub credentials stored via the macOS auth config path and XDG auth paths were being ignored. Fixed. (#53034)

Application Support path. The local ClawHub login stored under macOS Application Support wasn’t being read, even though XDG config was still honored. Now both paths work. Thanks @scoootscooob. (#52949)

Gateway skill browsing. The local ClawHub auth token wasn’t resolving for gateway-side skill browsing, and browse-all requests were hitting the wrong endpoint. Switched to search. Thanks @vincentkoc. (#52949)

If you were on macOS and openclaw plugins install clawhub:<package> silently failed or prompted for credentials you’d already saved — this is why.

Plugins: Messaging, Memory, and Config

Section titled “Plugins: Messaging, Memory, and Config”

Six fixes spanning the plugin surface. The common thread: optional things that stopped being optional, and initialization that happened too late.

Discord and Slack messaging. The message tool started requiring Discord components and Slack blocks that used to be optional. They’re optional again. Separately, Feishu message(..., media=...) sends now route through the outbound media path instead of failing silently. Thanks @vincentkoc. (#52970, #52962)

LanceDB memory plugin. First use of the memory-lancedb plugin would fail because LanceDB wasn’t bootstrapped into the plugin runtime state. Now it initializes on first access. (#26100)

Stale plugin config. If your plugins.allow list referenced a plugin id that no longer exists — renamed, removed, or typo — OpenClaw would refuse to start with a fatal config error. Now it warns and continues. Thanks @vincentkoc. (#52992)

DeepSeek refactor. The bundled DeepSeek provider has been refactored onto the shared single-provider plugin entry point, aligning it with other bundled providers. Thanks @07akioni. (#48762)

Matrix duplicate exports. Under Jiti, the Matrix plugin was exporting duplicate resolveMatrixAccountStringValues runtime-api entries, causing load failures. Fixed. Thanks @vincentkoc. (#52909, #52891)

Models and Providers: Token Limits, Pricing Loops, and Proxy Gaps

Section titled “Models and Providers: Token Limits, Pricing Loops, and Proxy Gaps”

Mistral token defaults. Bundled Mistral max-token defaults were set above safe output budgets, causing truncated or rejected completions. Lowered to safe values. openclaw doctor --fix now repairs old persisted Mistral provider configs automatically. Thanks @vincentkoc. (#52599)

OpenRouter pricing recursion. The openrouter/auto pricing refresh was recursing indefinitely during bootstrap. If your gateway was slow to start or you saw stack overflow traces on launch — this was it. Thanks @vincentkoc. (#53035)

Web search provider. The web_search agent tool was using a stale or default provider selection instead of the active runtime provider. Thanks @jzakirov. (#53020)

OpenAI Codex OAuth proxy. Two related fixes. The env-configured HTTP/HTTPS proxy dispatcher wasn’t initialized before stored-credential token renewal, and separately, it wasn’t initialized before OAuth preflight and token exchange. If you run OpenClaw behind a corporate proxy and use Codex OAuth or MiniMax OAuth, both paths now bootstrap the proxy dispatcher first. Thanks @openperf. (#52228; fixes #51619, #51569)

Channels: Telegram, Discord, WhatsApp, Plivo

Section titled “Channels: Telegram, Discord, WhatsApp, Plivo”

Telegram message ordering. Same-chat inbound messages were losing debounce order, and stale busy-session followups were getting stranded — never delivered, never timed out. Both fixed. Thanks @osolmaz. (#52998)

Telegram asDocument alias. forceDocument on image and GIF sends now has a user-facing asDocument alias. Small quality-of-life addition. Thanks @bakhtiersizhaev. (#52461)

Discord privileged commands. Native slash commands that require elevated permissions were failing silently. Now they return an explicit unauthorized reply. Thanks @scoootscooob. (#53041)

WhatsApp auto-enable. openclaw doctor auto-enable was appending built-in channel ids like whatsapp to plugins.allow, cluttering your config with entries that don’t belong there. Stopped. Thanks @vincentkoc. (#52931)

External channel catalogs. External channel catalogs can now override shipped fallback metadata, and overridden npm specs are honored during channel setup. (#52988)

Plivo voice replay. Plivo v2 replay keys were unstable — webhook retries collided with replay protection, causing dropped or duplicated voice call events. Keys are now stable. No more phantom replays.

Agents: Skills, Subagents, and Anthropic Transcripts

Section titled “Agents: Skills, Subagents, and Anthropic Transcripts”

Skill config resolution. Embedded skill config and env injection now prefer the active resolved runtime snapshot instead of a potentially stale one. Thanks @vincentkoc. (#53098)

Subagent timeouts. When a worker wait timed out, the completion event fired against a stale runtime snapshot. Now it rechecks the latest snapshot first. Thanks @vincentkoc. (#53106)

Anthropic transcript ordering. During transcript image sanitization, the ordering of assistant thinking and redacted-thinking blocks was getting shuffled. Preserved. Thanks @vincentkoc. (#52961)

Gateway and Security

Section titled “Gateway and Security”

Gateway probe timeouts. Successful gateway handshakes were timing out as “unreachable” while post-connect detail RPCs were still loading. The probe now distinguishes between a failed connect and a slow post-connect phase. Thanks @vincentkoc. (#52927)

Gateway crash loops. Lock conflicts were crash-looping the gateway under launchd and systemd. If you saw your gateway restart every few seconds in your service manager logs — fixed. Thanks @vincentkoc. (#52922)

Gateway auth hardening. Canvas routes now require auth. Agent session reset now requires admin scope. Both were unauthenticated before this fix.

Exec approval matching. Shell-wrapper positional-argv allowlist matching was incorrectly matching on non-direct carriers. Tightened to real direct carriers only. Thanks @vincentkoc.

Release packaging. Previously released bundled plugins and Control UI assets were missing from published openclaw npm installs. If you installed v2026.3.22 from npm and found missing UI assets or plugins — this is the fix. Thanks @vincentkoc.

Upgrade

Section titled “Upgrade”

Run openclaw doctor --fix after upgrading — it now repairs stale Mistral configs and cleans up spurious plugins.allow entries.

No breaking changes. No config migration needed. Drop-in replacement for v2026.3.22.

The Pattern

Section titled “The Pattern”

Massive releases produce massive surface area for bugs. That’s expected. What matters is the response time and the quality of community diagnostics.

@vincentkoc alone is credited on 18 of these 29 fixes. @scoootscooob, @osolmaz, @bakhtiersizhaev, @jzakirov, @openperf, and @07akioni each caught and helped resolve issues within hours of the release.

This is what a healthy open-source project looks like after a big ship: fast reports, fast fixes, no drama.

Full changelog: GitHub Release v2026.3.23

Twenty-nine fixes. Forty-eight hours. The biggest release needs the fastest follow-up.

OpenClaw v2026.3.22: Largest Release Ever — 10 Breaking Changes, 80+ Contributors, Full Security Overhaul

Mar 23, 2026
Vibe Sparking

OpenClaw v2026.3.22: Largest Release Ever

Section titled “OpenClaw v2026.3.22: Largest Release Ever”

Ten breaking changes in one release tag. If you run OpenClaw in production, read this before you run npm update.

This isn’t a typical feature dump. v2026.3.22 is the release where OpenClaw cleans house. The old Chrome extension relay, CLAWDBOT_* env vars, .moltbot state directories, the monolithic extension-api — all gone, with no compatibility shims.

Over 80 contributors made this happen.

Breaking Changes: Read This First

Section titled “Breaking Changes: Read This First”

ClawHub-first installs. openclaw plugins install <package> now checks ClawHub before npm. Falls back to npm only when ClawHub doesn’t have that package or version.

Chrome extension relay removed. The legacy Chrome extension relay path, bundled extension assets, driver: "extension", and browser.relayBindHost are gone. Run openclaw doctor --fix to migrate. Docker, headless, sandbox, and remote browser flows are unaffected.

Image generation standardized. The image_generate tool now handles both create and edit paths. Old nano-banana-pro docs and examples are removed. Switch to agents.defaults.imageGenerationModel.

New plugin SDK surface. The public SDK is now openclaw/plugin-sdk/*. openclaw/extension-api is deleted with no compatibility shim. Bundled plugins must use injected runtime for host-side operations.

Message discovery API change. ChannelMessageActionAdapter.describeMessageTool(...) is now the only way to do shared message tool discovery. Legacy listActions, getCapabilities, and getToolSchema are removed.

Matrix plugin rewritten. New Matrix plugin built on the official matrix-js-sdk. If upgrading from the previous plugin, follow the migration guide.

Legacy env names removed. All CLAWDBOT_* and MOLTBOT_* env names are removed from runtime, installers, and test tooling. Use the matching OPENCLAW_* names.

Legacy state dir removed. .moltbot state-dir and moltbot.json auto-detection are gone. Move to ~/.openclaw or set OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR.

Exec env sandbox hardening. Build-tool JVM injection (MAVEN_OPTS, SBT_OPTS, GRADLE_OPTS, ANT_OPTS), glibc tunable exploitation (GLIBC_TUNABLES), and .NET dependency resolution hijack (DOTNET_ADDITIONAL_DEPS) are blocked from the host exec environment. Gradle init script redirect is restricted to override-only.

Discord Carbon reconcile. Native command deployment defaults to Carbon reconcile. Discord restarts no longer churn slash commands through OpenClaw’s local deploy path.

Plugin Ecosystem: ClawHub and Bundles

Section titled “Plugin Ecosystem: ClawHub and Bundles”

ClawHub is now first-class. Native openclaw skills search|install|update flows, openclaw plugins install clawhub:<package> with tracked update metadata, and gateway support for ClawHub-backed requests.

Marketplace support. Claude marketplace registry resolution, plugin@marketplace installs, marketplace listing, and update support are live.

Bundle compatibility. Codex, Claude, and Cursor bundle discovery and install. Bundle skills map into OpenClaw skills. Claude bundle settings.json defaults apply to embedded Pi with shell overrides sanitized.

Hook management. Hook-pack install and update route through openclaw plugins. openclaw hooks focuses on hook visibility and per-hook controls.

Plugin commands. Owner-gated /plugins and /plugin chat commands for plugin list/show and enable/disable flows.

Models and Providers

Section titled “Models and Providers”

OpenAI default switch. Default OpenAI setup model switches to openai/gpt-5.4. Codex stays on openai-codex/gpt-5.4. Chat, image, TTS, transcription, and embedding defaults are centralized in one shared module.

GPT-5.4 family. Native forward-compat support for gpt-5.4-mini and gpt-5.4-nano.

Anthropic Vertex. Core anthropic-vertex provider for Claude via Google Vertex AI, including GCP auth and discovery.

Chutes provider. Bundled Chutes provider with plugin-owned OAuth/API-key auth and dynamic model discovery.

Web search providers. Exa, Tavily, and Firecrawl join as bundled web-search plugins with dedicated tools and config paths.

MiniMax M2.7. Default model bumps from M2.5 to M2.7. M2.7-highspeed added. /fast maps to highspeed variants. MiniMax API and OAuth plugins merged into a single default-on plugin.

xAI Grok updates. Bundled Grok catalog synced to current Pi-backed IDs, limits, and pricing. /fast maps to xAI Grok fast model family.

Z.AI GLM updates. Bundled GLM catalog synced to current Pi metadata, including 4.5/4.6 model families and updated pricing.

Xiaomi MiMo V2. Xiaomi provider switches to /v1 OpenAI-compatible endpoint. MiMo V2 Pro and MiMo V2 Omni added.

Agents and Sessions

Section titled “Agents and Sessions”

Per-agent thinking defaults. Per-agent thinking/reasoning/fast defaults with auto-revert for disallowed model overrides.

/btw side questions. Quick tool-less answers about the current session without changing future context. Dismissible in-session TUI answers, explicit BTW replies on external channels.

Compaction improvements. Users get notified when followup auto-compaction starts and finishes. Optional post-compaction session JSONL truncation drops summarized transcript entries. Default agent timeout raised from 600s to 48h.

Sandbox and Browser

Section titled “Sandbox and Browser”

Pluggable sandbox backends. OpenShell backend with mirror and remote workspace modes. SSH sandbox backend with secret-backed key, certificate, and known_hosts inputs. sandbox list/recreate/prune is now backend-aware.

Browser profiles. browser.profiles.<name>.userDataDir lets Chrome DevTools MCP attach to Brave, Edge, and other Chromium-based browsers.

Security Hardening

Section titled “Security Hardening”

The security section of this release is longer than most projects’ entire changelogs.

Windows SMB credential leak. Remote-host file:// media URLs and UNC/network paths are blocked before local filesystem resolution in core media loading and adjacent prompt/sandbox attachment seams.

Exec approval hardening. time is treated as a transparent dispatch wrapper — approvals bind the inner executable. Blank Hangul filler code points are escaped in approval prompts to prevent visually empty Unicode from hiding command text. macOS allowlist resolution hardened against wrapper and env spoofing. jq removed from default safe-bin allowlist.

Network security. Explicit-proxy SSRF pinning hardened for HTTPS proxy tunnels. Voice-call webhooks reject missing provider signature headers before body reads. Pre-auth body budget dropped to 64 KB/5s. Concurrent pre-auth requests per source IP are capped.

Device pairing. iOS setup codes bound to intended node profile. First-use bootstrap redemption that asks for broader roles is rejected.

Nostr/Synology Chat. Nostr DM policy enforced before decrypt with pre-crypto rate and size guards. Synology Chat reply delivery bound to stable numeric user_id by default.

Media security. Remote-media error-body snippets bounded with streaming caps and idle timeouts matching successful downloads.

Messaging Platforms

Section titled “Messaging Platforms”

Telegram. Auto-rename DM forum topics, per-account custom Bot API endpoints, silent error replies setting, hard-timeout stuck polling. New setups default to requireMention=true.

Feishu. Structured interactive approval and quick-action launcher cards, current-conversation ACP and subagent session binding, streaming reasoning token rendering, identity-aware structured card headers and footers.

Discord. Strict DM component allowlist auth. allow_sending_without_reply on reply-targeted sends.

Mattermost. replyToMode: "off" honored for threaded posts. DM delivery retries with configurable backoff.

Mobile

Section titled “Mobile”

Android dark theme. System-aware dark theme across onboarding and chat flows. Talk speech synthesis moved behind gateway. Call log and SMS search support added.

Control UI

Section titled “Control UI”

Canvas expand. Expand-to-canvas button on assistant chat bubbles with in-app session navigation.

Appearance settings. Unified theme border radii with a Roundness slider to adjust corner radius from sharp to fully rounded.

Notable Fixes

Section titled “Notable Fixes”

Too many to list exhaustively. The ones with the biggest blast radius:

  • Gateway startup speed. Bundled channel plugins load from compiled dist entries. Cold starts drop from tens of seconds back to seconds. Primary model prewarmed before channel startup.
  • OpenAI-compatible tool calls. Duplicate tool_call_id values deduplicated. Third-party providers no longer reject with HTTP 400.
  • WhatsApp reconnect. Append recency filter restored. Protobuf Long timestamps handled correctly. Outbound listener state preserved across reconnects.
  • Compaction safety. Orphaned tool_result blocks repaired after session.compact(). Long tool loops trigger overflow recovery before next model call hard-fails.
  • Memory flush. Transcript-hash dedup stays active across memory-flush fallback retries. No more duplicate MEMORY.md entries.

Upgrade

Section titled “Upgrade”

Run openclaw doctor --fix after upgrading.

Breaking change checklist:

  1. Check plugin installs — ClawHub is now the default source
  2. Chrome extension relay users — removed, use existing-session or user driver
  3. nano-banana-pro users — switch to agents.defaults.imageGenerationModel
  4. Plugin developers — migrate to openclaw/plugin-sdk/*
  5. Matrix users — follow migration guide for the new plugin
  6. CLAWDBOT_* / MOLTBOT_* env vars — rename to OPENCLAW_*
  7. ~/.moltbot state dir — move to ~/.openclaw
  8. Java/Gradle projects using host exec env vars — check sandbox block list
  9. Discord slash command deployment changed — Carbon reconcile is the new default
  10. Message tool discovery API changed — migrate to describeMessageTool(...)

Full Changelog

Section titled “Full Changelog”

See the GitHub Release for the complete list of PRs and contributors.

Ten breaking changes. Eighty-plus contributors. One house-cleaning release. Some versions add features. This one defines direction.

Claude Code 2.1.78: The Trust Release -- Plugins Get State, Silent Failures Get Loud

Mar 18, 2026
Vibe Sparking

Claude Code 2.1.78: The Trust Release — Plugins Get State, Silent Failures Get Loud

Section titled “Claude Code 2.1.78: The Trust Release — Plugins Get State, Silent Failures Get Loud”

Your AI coding assistant crashed mid-task because the API rate-limited you. The turn ended. No hook fired. No cleanup ran. You found out when you came back from coffee and saw a dead terminal.

That was 2.1.77. In 2.1.78, there’s a StopFailure hook event for exactly this. One line in a changelog. A whole class of silent failures, gone.

At a glance

Section titled “At a glance”
AreaWhat changed
HooksNew StopFailure event fires when a turn ends due to API errors (rate limit, auth failure)
Plugins${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_DATA} for persistent state that survives updates; uninstall prompts before deleting
Plugin agentseffort, maxTurns, disallowedTools frontmatter support
StreamingResponse text streams line-by-line as generated
tmuxTerminal notifications reach outer terminal with set -g allow-passthrough on
SandboxNo longer silently disables when dependencies missing — shows startup warning
MCPdeny: ["mcp__servername"] now actually removes tools before sending to model
Security.git, .claude directories no longer writable without prompt in bypassPermissions mode
Gitlog HEAD no longer fails in sandboxed Bash; stub files no longer pollute git status
Sessionscc log and --resume no longer truncate history on large sessions (>5 MB)
StabilityInfinite loop from stop hooks re-feeding API errors to model is fixed
VoiceWorks on WSL2 with WSLg; clear error on WSL1/Win10
Keyboardctrl+u does readline kill-line in normal mode again (scroll moved to transcript mode)
PATHBash tool finds Homebrew binaries when VS Code launches from Dock/Spotlight
DisplayClaude orange color no longer washed out in terminals without truecolor
ModelsANTHROPIC_CUSTOM_MODEL_OPTION env var adds custom entry to /model picker
VS CodeNo login screen flash; model dropdown hides 1M context variant for unsupported tiers

The pattern beneath the changelog

Section titled “The pattern beneath the changelog”

Changelogs are strange documents. Every line is a fix or a feature, but the interesting part is never any single line. It’s the pattern across all of them.

Claude Code 2.1.78 shipped with 25+ changes. It looks like a bug-fix release. Read closer and a different picture emerges: this is a trust and reliability release. Almost every change addresses a scenario where Claude Code did something unexpected, failed silently, or left the developer guessing.

Three threads run through the update.

Thread 1: Plugins get real infrastructure

Section titled “Thread 1: Plugins get real infrastructure”

Plugins now get persistent state through the ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_DATA} variable. This data survives plugin updates. The /plugin uninstall command prompts before deleting it.

Plugin-shipped agents gained frontmatter support for effort, maxTurns, and disallowedTools. Plugin authors can now ship agents that constrain themselves — declare their resource budget and tool restrictions up front.

These changes aren’t user-facing features. They’re platform-level infrastructure. The message to plugin authors: build here, your state is safe, your agents have proper controls.

Thread 2: Silent failures become loud ones

Section titled “Thread 2: Silent failures become loud ones”

This is the most telling thread. Count how many fixes follow the same pattern: something failed quietly, now it fails loudly or doesn’t fail at all.

Sandbox silently disabled. When sandbox.enabled: true was set but dependencies were missing, the sandbox just… didn’t run. No error. No warning. You thought you had sandboxing. You didn’t. Now there’s a visible startup warning.

MCP deny rules ignored. deny: ["mcp__servername"] permission rules weren’t removing blocked tools from what the model could see. The model would notice the tool, try to use it, and fail. The deny rule existed but didn’t work as expected. Fixed — tools are now removed before sending to the model.

Sandbox paths broken. sandbox.filesystem.allowWrite didn’t work with absolute paths. You needed a // prefix that was undocumented. Now absolute paths work directly.

Protected directories exposed. .git, .claude, and other protected directories were writable without a prompt in bypassPermissions mode. A mode designed to trust the user was also trusting the AI with sensitive directories. Fixed.

Infinite loop. API errors could trigger stop hooks that re-fed blocking errors to the model, creating an infinite loop. The kind of bug that makes you wonder how long your machine was spinning before you noticed.

Git status pollution. git log HEAD failed with an “ambiguous argument” error inside sandboxed Bash on Linux. Stub files polluted git status in the working directory.

Session truncation. cc log and --resume silently truncated conversation history on large sessions (>5 MB) that used subagents. Your conversation history was there, but the tool only showed you part of it.

Each of these is a scenario where a developer lost time or trust because the tool didn’t tell them what was happening.

Thread 3: Edge cases from real workflows

Section titled “Thread 3: Edge cases from real workflows”

These aren’t theoretical bugs from a test matrix. They’re friction points from actual daily use.

Voice mode on WSL2. Wasn’t working with WSLg on Windows 11. WSL1/Win10 users now get a clear error instead of mysterious silence.

Ctrl+u. In normal mode, ctrl+u was scrolling the view instead of doing readline kill-line (clearing the input before cursor). The keybinding collision is resolved — half-page scroll with ctrl+u/ctrl+d moved to transcript mode only.

Voice modifier keys. Push-to-talk keybindings like ctrl+k required a hold instead of activating immediately. Fixed.

Homebrew PATH. The Bash tool couldn’t find Homebrew and other PATH-dependent binaries when VS Code was launched from Dock or Spotlight on macOS. A PATH inheritance issue that only happens in certain launch contexts.

Washed-out color. The Claude orange color appeared washed out in VS Code, Cursor, and code-server terminals that don’t advertise truecolor support.

Worktree loading. The --worktree flag wasn’t loading skills and hooks from the worktree directory.

Wrong platform info. The /sandbox Dependencies tab showed Linux prerequisites on macOS.

Git instructions setting. CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_GIT_INSTRUCTIONS and the includeGitInstructions setting weren’t actually suppressing the git status section in the system prompt.

Fixing these says: we test in the environments our users actually run in, not just the ones that are convenient.

Streaming gets smoother

Section titled “Streaming gets smoother”

Response text now streams line-by-line as it’s generated. Technically a performance improvement. Experientially, it changes the tool from “waiting for an answer” to “watching it think.” That difference in feel matters.

Queued prompts are also no longer concatenated without a newline separator — a small formatting fix that was probably maddening for anyone who hit it.

Smaller additions worth knowing

Section titled “Smaller additions worth knowing”

Custom model picker entries. ANTHROPIC_CUSTOM_MODEL_OPTION env var adds a custom entry to the /model picker. Optional _NAME and _DESCRIPTION suffixed vars control display. Useful for custom fine-tunes or proxies.

tmux notifications. Terminal notifications (iTerm2, Kitty, Ghostty popups, progress bar) now reach the outer terminal inside tmux. Requires set -g allow-passthrough on in your tmux config.

Session performance. Memory usage and startup time improved when resuming large sessions.

ANTHROPIC_BETAS. The environment variable was being silently ignored when using Haiku models. Fixed.

VS Code specific

Section titled “VS Code specific”

Two VS Code fixes:

  1. The brief flash of the login screen when opening the sidebar while already authenticated is gone.
  2. The model dropdown no longer offers the 1M context Opus variant to subscribers whose plan tier is unknown — you won’t see “API Error: Rate limit reached” when selecting Opus anymore.

What this release is really about

Section titled “What this release is really about”

Bug-fix releases don’t tell exciting stories. But they tell honest ones.

2.1.78 is the kind of release that happens when a tool graduates from impressive to reliable. The plugin infrastructure says: we’re building a platform, not just a product. The failure transparency says: we’d rather show you an error than hide a problem. The edge-case fixes say: we’re listening to what actually goes wrong, not just what looks good in demos.

If you depend on Claude Code for daily work, update. Not for any single feature. For the cumulative effect of 25+ things that now work the way you assumed they already did.

OpenClaw v2026.3.13-1: Recovery Release Ships 70+ Fixes Across Agents, Security, Mobile, and Messaging

Mar 17, 2026
Vibe Sparking

OpenClaw v2026.3.13-1: Recovery Release Ships 70+ Fixes

Section titled “OpenClaw v2026.3.13-1: Recovery Release Ships 70+ Fixes”

GitHub won’t let you reuse a published release tag. When v2026.3.13 shipped broken, the team couldn’t just fix and re-push. So they tagged v2026.3.13-1, kept npm at 2026.3.13, and packed 70+ fixes into what became one of the most community-driven releases in the project’s history.

Why v2026.3.13-1?

Section titled “Why v2026.3.13-1?”

The original v2026.3.13 tag and GitHub Release broke. GitHub’s immutable release system prevents overwriting published tags. The solution:

  • Git tag / GitHub Release: v2026.3.13-1
  • npm package version: 2026.3.13 (unchanged)

The -1 suffix exists only for Git and GitHub. If you install via npm, nothing changes.

Agent fixes: the big ones

Section titled “Agent fixes: the big ones”

The agent layer received the most attention this cycle.

Thinking block replay. Anthropic thinking blocks were being replayed incorrectly during agent conversations. Fixed — they’re now dropped on replay (#44843).

Memory file double-injection. On case-insensitive file systems (macOS, Windows), memory files could get injected twice into agent context. Path comparison now handles case folding (#26054).

Session reset preservation. lastAccountId and lastThreadId were getting wiped on session reset. They’re preserved now (#44773). The reset prompt was also reworded to avoid triggering Azure content filters (#43403).

Cross-agent workspace resolution. When an agent spawned a subagent targeting a different agent’s workspace, the target path resolved incorrectly. Fixed (#40176).

Custom provider keys. Blank local API keys for custom providers were getting overwritten during onboarding. They’re preserved now (#45631).

Post-compaction sanity check. The compaction system now uses the full-session token count instead of a partial count for its sanity check (#28347).

Security hardening

Section titled “Security hardening”

Docker token leak. Gateway tokens could leak through the Docker build context. The Dockerfiles now prevent this (#44956). All Dockerfiles also add apt-get upgrade for base image security (#45384).

Control-UI auth. The auth bypass for insecure control-ui connections was accidentally removed. Restored, with proper connect failure classification (#45512).

macOS PortGuard. PortGuard was killing Docker Desktop processes when running in remote mode. It no longer does (#13798).

Shared auth on insecure connects. Shared auth state is now maintained on insecure control-ui connections (#45088).

Gateway token requests. Unanswered client requests are now bounded to prevent resource exhaustion (#45689).

Messaging platform fixes

Section titled “Messaging platform fixes”

Telegram. Inbound media downloads now retry over IPv4 fallback when IPv6 fails (#45327). Thread media transport policy is properly threaded into SSRF protection (#44639).

Feishu. Non-ASCII filenames are preserved in file uploads (#34262). An early event-level dedup layer prevents duplicate replies — if you’ve been seeing double messages, this is the fix (#43762).

Discord. Gateway metadata fetch failures no longer crash the handler (#44397).

Signal. Groups config is now part of the Signal channel schema (#27199).

Slack. Opt-in interactive reply directives let you build richer Slack integrations (#44607, #45463). The redundant ?? undefined in the Slack probe was cleaned up (#44775).

Mobile clients

Section titled “Mobile clients”

Android got a redesigned chat settings UI (#44894), a fix for HttpURLConnection leaks in TalkModeVoiceResolver (#43780), Google Code Scanner for onboarding QR codes (#45021), and a missing params field in the agent validation schema (#41171).

iOS ships an onboarding welcome pager (#45054).

Browser automation

Section titled “Browser automation”

The browser tool received three fixes for batch action dispatch. Selector and batch support are normalized (#45457). Batch failure and limit handling are hardened (#45506). Existing-session driver validation and session lifecycle management are tightened (#45682).

Build and UI

Section titled “Build and UI”

Memory regression. Plugin-sdk chunks were being duplicated, causing a roughly 2x memory regression. Fixed via deduplication (#45426).

Dashboard reload storm. Chat history was reloading in a loop on the dashboard. Stopped (#45541).

Chat rendering. Oversized chat replies stay readable (#45559). The scroll pill button got its chat-new-messages CSS class back (#44856). Chat context notice icon sizing was fixed (#45533).

Ollama. Native reasoning-only output is hidden for Ollama models (#45330).

Gemini. Model-id normalization now applies to the google-vertex provider too (#42435).

Other notable changes

Section titled “Other notable changes”
  • Cron deadlocks. Isolated cron nested lane deadlocks are prevented (#45459).
  • Plugin collisions. Plugins now fail fast on channel and binding collisions (#45628).
  • Timezone support. Docker containers support OPENCLAW_TZ for timezone configuration (#34119).
  • macOS exec approvals. exec-approvals.json settings are now respected in the gateway prompter (#13707).
  • Persona continuity. Compaction summaries preserve persona and language continuity (#10456).
  • Brave costs. Incorrect rendering of Brave costs in docs was fixed (#44989).
  • Sidebar polish. Sidebar status, agent skills, and chat rendering got a polish pass (#45451).
  • Updater refresh. The updater service refresh now guards against missing invocation cwd (#45486).
  • Default model update. Tests updated from openai-codex/gpt-5.3-codex to openai-codex/gpt-5.4 (#44367).
  • Gateway probe. Scope-limited probe RPC is treated as degraded reachability (#45622).
  • Session transcript. chat.inject now creates the transcript file when missing (#36645).
  • Discovery config. Missing domain added to wideArea Zod config schema (#35615).
  • Firecrawl config. Web fetch firecrawl config restored in runtime Zod schema (#42583).
  • Delivery dedup. Review follow-ups for delivery dedup were addressed (#44666).
  • Anthropic startup crash. A config-related crash on Anthropic startup was fixed (#45520).

Upgrade

Section titled “Upgrade”

Docker users: rebuild your images. The apt-get upgrade addition and token leak fix are worth it.

If you use Feishu and have been getting duplicate replies, this release fixes it. If you self-host behind a reverse proxy, the control-ui auth restore matters.

Full changelog

Section titled “Full changelog”

See the GitHub Release for the complete list of PRs and contributors.

70+ fixes. Dozens of contributors. One recovery tag. This is what open source looks like when the community shows up.

OpenClaw v2026.3.11: WebSocket Hijacking Patched, Ollama Gets First-Class Setup, Memory Goes Multimodal

Mar 12, 2026
Vibe Sparking

OpenClaw v2026.3.11: WebSocket Hijacking Patched, Ollama Gets First-Class Setup, Memory Goes Multimodal

Section titled “OpenClaw v2026.3.11: WebSocket Hijacking Patched, Ollama Gets First-Class Setup, Memory Goes Multimodal”

A cross-site WebSocket hijacking path in trusted-proxy mode could hand operator.admin access to untrusted origins. That’s patched now. But the security fix is just the opener for one of OpenClaw’s largest releases — 56 commits touching nearly every subsystem.

Security: upgrade immediately

Section titled “Security: upgrade immediately”

GHSA-5wcw-8jjv-m286. The Gateway’s WebSocket handler now enforces browser origin validation for all browser-originated connections, regardless of whether proxy headers are present. Previously, in trusted-proxy mode, the origin check could be skipped. An attacker on an untrusted origin could establish a WebSocket connection and gain operator.admin scope.

If you run OpenClaw behind a reverse proxy, upgrade before doing anything else.

Ollama: proper onboarding at last

Section titled “Ollama: proper onboarding at last”

Setting up Ollama with OpenClaw used to mean editing config files and guessing which models to pull. That’s over.

The new onboarding flow offers two modes:

  • Local — everything runs on your machine
  • Cloud + Local — browser-based cloud sign-in paired with local model inference

You get curated model suggestions during setup. Cloud models skip unnecessary local pulls. The wizard handles it.

This also introduces the OpenCode Go provider — a new Go-based runtime. Zen and Go share one OpenCode key but keep their runtime providers separate. If you’re already using OpenCode Zen, the existing key works for Go too.

Memory goes multimodal

Section titled “Memory goes multimodal”

Memory search was text-only. Now it handles images and audio.

Enable opt-in multimodal indexing for memorySearch.extraPaths using Gemini’s gemini-embedding-2-preview. Configure output dimensions per your needs. When dimensions change, the index rebuilds automatically. Scope-based reindexing keeps things efficient — only changed scopes get re-embedded.

For the Gemini embedding backend specifically, gemini-embedding-2-preview support includes configurable output dimensions and automatic reindex on dimension changes. Two separate PRs landed for this, from different contributors, both now merged.

iOS: rebuilt from the home screen up

Section titled “iOS: rebuilt from the home screen up”

Three changes ship together:

  1. Welcome screen. A bundled home view with a live agent overview. Refreshes on connect, reconnect, and foreground return.
  2. Docked toolbar. Floating controls are gone. The compact connection pill moved off the top-left overlay.
  3. Chat opens in the right session. Chat now opens in the resolved main session instead of a synthetic ios session.

Also fixed: the app no longer stays disconnected after returning from background. Previous behavior required waiting for a later wake path — now it reconnects immediately when foreground returns after stale background sockets are torn down.

A local beta release flow with Fastlane support also landed, covering prepare, archive, and upload to TestFlight.

macOS: chat model picker

Section titled “macOS: chat model picker”

The macOS client adds a chat model picker in the shared chat composer. Explicit thinking-level selections persist across relaunch. Provider-aware session model sync is hardened for the shared composer path.

The onboarding flow now detects when remote gateways need a shared auth token and explains where to find it on the gateway host — including when a successful check used paired-device auth instead.

Breaking: cron job isolation

Section titled “Breaking: cron job isolation”

Cron jobs can no longer notify through ad hoc agent sends or fallback main-session summaries. This is deliberate tightening of isolated cron delivery.

Run openclaw doctor --fix to migrate legacy cron storage and legacy notify/webhook delivery metadata.

If you have cron jobs that relied on sending messages through agent sends as a side channel, they’ll stop working. The migration path is explicit.

Gateway auth hardening

Section titled “Gateway auth hardening”

Multiple security fixes landed across the auth stack:

  • SecretRef traversal rejection. Exec SecretRef traversal IDs rejected across schema, runtime, and gateway.
  • Fail closed on missing SecretRefs. Local gateway.auth.* SecretRefs that are unavailable now fail closed instead of silently falling back to gateway.remote.* credentials.
  • Config write scoping. /config and /allowlist edits now enforce configWrites against both originating and targeted account scopes, blocking sibling-account mutations.
  • Session reset auth split. Conversation /new and /reset split from the admin-only sessions.reset control-plane RPC.
  • Plugin runtime auth. Unauthenticated plugin HTTP routes no longer inherit synthetic admin gateway scopes.
  • Sandbox session-tree visibility. Session-tree visibility and agent-to-agent access guards enforced before reading or mutating target session state.

Model and agent fixes

Section titled “Model and agent fixes”

Leaked model control tokens stripped. GLM-5 and DeepSeek internal delimiters (<|...|> and full-width variants) no longer reach end users.

Fallback improvements. HTTP 499 (Anthropic client-closed overload), Venice 402 (insufficient balance), Poe 402 (used up points), and Gemini MALFORMED_RESPONSE stop reasons all now trigger model fallback correctly.

Cooldown fix. Expired auth-profile cooldown counters reset properly instead of re-escalating into long loops. Default cooldown windows with no failure history report as unknown instead of rate_limit.

Kimi Coding fix. Tools sent in native Anthropic format again — kimi-coding was degrading tool calls into XML/plain-text pseudo invocations.

Telegram: four delivery fixes

Section titled “Telegram: four delivery fixes”
  1. Final preview delivery. Split active preview lifecycle from cleanup retention to avoid duplicate fallback sends.
  2. First-preview edge case. Ambiguous missing-message_id finals handled correctly for first-preview/no-id cases.
  3. Stale cleanup-retain. Archived-preview retains no longer leave stale partial bubbles beside fallback-sent finals.
  4. Outbound HTML chunking. Long HTML messages chunk correctly, with plain-text fallback when HTML chunk planning can’t safely preserve the full message.

ACP: ten patches

Section titled “ACP: ten patches”

The Agent Communication Protocol got heavy attention:

  • resumeSessionId for spawned ACP sessions
  • Main session alias canonicalization (main before lookup)
  • Image attachment forwarding into ACP runtime turns
  • Session restore and prompt completion degrade gracefully on failures
  • Tool streaming with text content and file-location hints
  • Gateway-backed session controls and metadata exposure
  • Stop reason mapping: error completions resolve as end_turn instead of refusal
  • Mode change rejections propagated instead of silent success
  • Implicit streaming for mode="run" spawns to eligible parent sessions
  • ACPX pin bumped to 0.1.16

Everything else

Section titled “Everything else”

Discord. autoArchiveDuration channel config for auto-created threads. Runtime config threading for SecretRef-based credentials.

Mattermost. First-line indentation preserved when stripping bot mentions. Native table rendering instead of fenced-code fallback.

MS Teams. General channel conversation ID used as resolved team key for allowlist matching.

Signal. channels.signal.accountUuid accepted in strict config validation.

Feishu. Local image paths upload as Feishu images again via mediaLocalRoots.

CLI. ANSI/C1 control bytes stripped from skills list --json. ASCII table borders default on legacy Windows consoles. Memory search/index managers closed in one-shot CLI shutdown.

Sandbox. Staged writes pinned to verified parent directories. TAR extraction hardened against symlink escapes.

Upgrade

Section titled “Upgrade”

Run openclaw doctor --fix after upgrade to migrate legacy cron storage if you use cron jobs.

The security fix alone makes this a mandatory upgrade for anyone running OpenClaw with browser access behind a reverse proxy.

Google Antigravity Terminal Sandboxing: AI Agents Finally Won't Delete Your Files

Jan 28, 2026
Vibe Sparking

Google Antigravity Terminal Sandboxing: AI Agents Finally Won’t Delete Your Files

Section titled “Google Antigravity Terminal Sandboxing: AI Agents Finally Won’t Delete Your Files”

Google Antigravity has just rolled out a terminal sandbox feature that addresses a very practical problem in agentic AI development: AI agents executing commands in the terminal will no longer accidentally mess with your system files.

The Problem AI Agents Created

Section titled “The Problem AI Agents Created”

When you give an AI agent terminal access, powerful things become possible. The agent can install dependencies, run tests, build projects, and deploy code. But this power comes with risk.

A simple mistake could lead to:

  • Accidentally deleting system files
  • Modifying configurations outside the project
  • Breaking your development environment
  • Running commands in unintended directories

This isn’t hypothetical—developers have experienced these issues firsthand when trusting autonomous agents with unrestricted terminal access.

How the Sandbox Works

Section titled “How the Sandbox Works”

The terminal sandbox employs kernel-level isolation technology, strictly confining all AI agent terminal commands within the project working directory.

As Google’s documentation states:

“When sandboxing is enabled, the Agent’s terminal commands are subject to the following restrictions: File System: Commands can only write to your designated workspace directory and essential system locations.”

Technical Implementation

Section titled “Technical Implementation”

Currently, this feature is implemented on macOS through Apple’s Seatbelt mechanism (sandbox-exec), providing kernel-level sandboxing. Linux support is planned for future releases.

The sandbox creates a designated playground for AI — it can only operate within the folder you specify. Network access can also be controlled independently, giving you fine-grained control over what your agent can do.

Enabling the Feature

Section titled “Enabling the Feature”

The sandbox is currently opt-in (though this may change in future releases):

  1. Open Antigravity Settings
  2. Find “Terminal Sandboxing”
  3. Toggle “Enable Terminal Sandboxing”
  4. Configure network access permissions as needed

Why This Feature Matters

Section titled “Why This Feature Matters”

One user highlighted a common scenario:

“I need AI agents to work on code repositories while also organizing my computer files.”

This type of need is typical but carries significant risks without sandbox protection. The feature enables developers to:

  • Trust agents more freely – Work across multiple projects without constant worry
  • Safely vibe code – Give the IDE broader access when the sandbox protects the terminal
  • Isolate project work – Keep agent activity contained within specific directories

Early User Feedback

Section titled “Early User Feedback”

Not everything is perfect. Early adopters have reported some friction:

Deepak from DeepakNess noted that the sandbox “constantly asks me to run commands like sudo chown -R 501:20 "/Users/deepak/.npm"” and ultimately chose to disable it:

“The terminal sandboxing feature in Antigravity is annoying as hell… I am turning this feature off.”

This feedback highlights the trade-off between security and convenience. Sandbox restrictions can interfere with legitimate package manager operations and other development workflows.

The Bigger Picture

Section titled “The Bigger Picture”

Terminal sandboxing represents a maturing of the agentic AI landscape. As we move from “AI as copilot” to “AI as autonomous agent,” safety mechanisms become essential.

This is particularly relevant given recent Chrome sandbox escape vulnerabilities (CVE-2025-2783, CVE-2025-13097) that demonstrate how difficult sandbox security truly is. Google’s decision to sandbox terminal commands shows they understand the stakes.

Best Practices

Section titled “Best Practices”

Until sandboxing is perfected, consider:

  1. Test in isolated environments – Use Docker containers or VMs for risky operations
  2. Review commands before execution – Many agents offer approval workflows
  3. Keep backups – Always have recovery options when working with autonomous agents
  4. Provide feedback – Report issues to help improve the feature

Looking Forward

Section titled “Looking Forward”

The current implementation is macOS-only, with Linux coming soon. The default-off setting may change as the feature matures.

For now, terminal sandboxing in Google Antigravity is a significant step toward safer agentic AI development. It acknowledges the real risks of autonomous terminal access while providing a path toward making agents trustworthy development partners.

Vibe Sparking

Superagent: AI Guardrails for Secure and Compliant Agents

Section titled “Superagent: AI Guardrails for Secure and Compliant Agents”

As AI agents and chatbots become integral to business operations, ensuring their security and compliance has never been more critical. Enter Superagent – an open-source guardrail system that provides purpose-trained models to secure AI applications in real-time.

The Challenge of AI Safety

Section titled “The Challenge of AI Safety”

Building production AI applications introduces unique security challenges:

  • Prompt injection attacks that can hijack agent behavior
  • Hallucinations that spread misinformation
  • Data leaks through inadvertent PII/PHI exposure
  • Compliance violations across regulatory frameworks
  • Tool abuse where agents execute unauthorized actions

Traditional approaches using general-purpose LLMs for safety checks introduce latency and lack the precision needed for production environments.

What is Superagent?

Section titled “What is Superagent?”

Superagent provides three purpose-trained models that work together to secure AI applications:

Guard

Section titled “Guard”

Threat Detection with 98% Accuracy

Guard detects and blocks unsafe inputs before they reach your models:

  • Prompt injections and jailbreak attempts
  • Malicious tool calls
  • Backdoors and adversarial inputs
  • Unsafe content generation

According to Superagent’s benchmarks, Guard outperforms GPT-4, Gemini 2.5 Pro, and other frontier models in threat detection – without the latency penalty of running a full LLM for safety checks.

Verify

Section titled “Verify”

Output Validation and Grounding

Verify grounds and validates model outputs against enterprise sources:

  • Fact-checking against internal documents
  • Policy compliance verification
  • Consistency validation
  • Hallucination prevention

Every generation is validated before reaching users, ensuring factual accuracy and policy alignment.

Redact

Section titled “Redact”

Real-Time Data Protection

Redact removes sensitive data from text and documents:

  • PII (Personally Identifiable Information)
  • PHI (Protected Health Information)
  • API keys and secrets
  • Custom sensitive patterns

Privacy and compliance are maintained across AI inputs and outputs without manual review.

Unlike general-purpose LLMs used for safety, Superagent’s models are purpose-trained for specific security tasks, enabling:

MCP Defender: Docker's New AI Agent Security Shield

Dec 25, 2025
Vibe Sparking

Docker Acquires MCP Defender: The Security Layer AI Agents Have Been Missing

As AI agents become increasingly autonomous in our development workflows, the security landscape has fundamentally shifted. Enter MCP Defender—a desktop app that Docker recently acquired to protect AI applications like Cursor, Claude Desktop, VS Code, and Windsurf from a growing array of attacks.

1. What is MCP Defender?

Section titled “1. What is MCP Defender?”

MCP Defender is a desktop application that acts as a security proxy for the Model Context Protocol (MCP). Here’s how it works:

  • 🛡️ Automatic Protection: All MCP tool call requests and responses from AI apps are automatically proxied through MCP Defender
  • 🔎 Signature-Based Detection: Intercepted data is checked against a set of security signatures
  • 🔐 User-Controlled Blocking: When harmful content is detected, MCP Defender alerts you and asks whether to allow or block the tool call

Supported AI Apps:

  • Cursor
  • Claude Desktop
  • Visual Studio Code
  • Windsurf

2. Why Docker Acquired MCP Defender

Section titled “2. Why Docker Acquired MCP Defender”

On September 5, 2025, Docker announced the acquisition of MCP Defender, marking a strategic move into AI agent security. The rationale is clear:

“AI agents are getting smarter—and more autonomous. That means new risks, new attack surfaces, and a need for runtime security that moves as fast as dev teams do.”

The Security Gap

Section titled “The Security Gap”

Traditional security tools weren’t designed for AI agents. When an AI agent has the ability to:

  • Execute code
  • Access file systems
  • Make API calls
  • Interact with external services

…the attack surface expands dramatically. MCP Defender fills this critical gap by providing:

CapabilityDescription
Runtime MonitoringContinuous observation of AI agent behavior
Policy EnforcementCustomizable security rules for AI operations
Real-time Threat DetectionIdentifies malicious patterns as they occur
Multi-Client ProtectionSecures multiple AI apps simultaneously

3. Getting Started

Section titled “3. Getting Started”

Quick Install (Mac)

Section titled “Quick Install (Mac)”

Download the latest release directly:

  • Download MCP Defender for Mac

From Source

Section titled “From Source”

Once running, MCP Defender automatically intercepts MCP traffic from supported AI apps—no additional configuration needed.

4. How It Protects You

Section titled “4. How It Protects You”

MCP Defender guards against several attack vectors:

🔴 Prompt Injection Attacks

Section titled “🔴 Prompt Injection Attacks”

Malicious instructions embedded in data that trick AI agents into executing harmful commands.

🔴 Data Exfiltration

Section titled “🔴 Data Exfiltration”

Prevents unauthorized data extraction through AI tool calls.

🔴 Unauthorized Tool Execution

Section titled “🔴 Unauthorized Tool Execution”

Blocks attempts to execute tools or commands beyond the intended scope.

🔴 Supply Chain Attacks

Section titled “🔴 Supply Chain Attacks”

Detects compromised MCP servers or malicious tool definitions.

5. Docker’s Security Vision

Section titled “5. Docker’s Security Vision”

The acquisition fits into Docker’s broader “secure-by-default AI infrastructure” vision:

  • Docker Scout: Container image vulnerability scanning
  • Docker Hardened Images: Pre-secured base images
  • Docker MCP Gateway: Secure MCP server hosting
  • MCP Defender: Runtime AI agent protection

Together, these tools aim to defend the entire AI software supply chain while reducing the security burden on development teams.

6. Real-World Demo

Section titled “6. Real-World Demo”

MCP Defender has demonstrated its value against real attack scenarios:

Attack TypeHow MCP Defender Responds
WhatsApp Data ExfiltrationBlocks unauthorized access to messaging data
File System ManipulationAlerts when AI attempts to access sensitive directories
Code Injection via Tool CallsIntercepts and flags malicious payloads

The app shows a clear alert dialog when threats are detected, giving you full control over whether to allow or block the action.

7. Final Thoughts

Section titled “7. Final Thoughts”

AI agents are transforming how we build software, but with great power comes great responsibility—and greater attack surfaces. MCP Defender represents a crucial evolution in AI security:

  • For Individual Developers: Peace of mind when using AI coding assistants
  • For Enterprise Teams: Compliance-ready AI agent governance
  • For the Ecosystem: A foundation for secure agentic AI infrastructure

With Docker’s backing, MCP Defender is positioned to become the standard for AI agent security. If you’re using Cursor, Claude Desktop, VS Code, or Windsurf, installing MCP Defender is now a no-brainer.
